posts.title: MCP Elicitation: The Server Asks, the User Answers
posts.subtitle: The primitive that lets a server pause mid-call and request exactly the input it's missing.
posts.summary: Elicitation lets an MCP server pause a tool call and send the client a JSON-Schema-described question, so the human — not the model — supplies the missing piece. Responses come back as accept, decline, or cancel, and the spec deliberately restricts schemas to flat primitive fields and bans requesting sensitive data through the channel.

slides.title: A Tool Call That Stops and Asks a Question
slides.body: MCP elicitation lets a server pause mid-operation and request structured input directly from the human, through the client — no model guessing required.

slides.title: Before Elicitation, a Server Could Only Fail or Guess
bullets: A deploy tool needs a target environment name the model never provided; a booking server needs a date the user forgot to mention; a destructive action needs explicit confirmation.

Without a way to ask, the server had three bad options: fail with an error and make the model re-guess, silently pick a default, or require every parameter to be configured up front at connection time.
Any of those breaks the moment a workflow is genuinely interactive — the missing piece lives in the human's head, not in the conversation so far.

slides.title: elicitation/create Sends a Schema, Not Free Text
bullets: A client that supports the feature declares an `elicitation` capability at initialization; a server can then send an `elicitation/create` request mid-call with a human-readable `message` and a `requestedSchema`.

That schema is deliberately restricted to a flat object of primitive properties only — strings, numbers, booleans, enums — with constraints like minLength or format: email. No nested objects, no arrays of objects.
The client renders that schema as an actual form (or CLI prompt) instead of just piping text back to the model, so the human fills in exactly the fields the server asked for.

slides.title: Three Outcomes, Not Two: Accept, Decline, Cancel
bullets: accept: the user explicitly submitted data — the response carries a content object matching the requested schema.
decline: the user explicitly refused the request — content is omitted, and the server should treat this as a real 'no', not a retry-able failure.
cancel: the user dismissed the dialog without choosing — content is omitted, and the server should treat this as inconclusive rather than a refusal.
The spec calls this out on purpose: humans get distracted, close dialogs, or come back later, and collapsing that into a boolean would lose information a well-behaved server actually needs.

slides.title: A CI Tool Confirms Before It Deletes a Branch
bullets: The model calls a `cleanup_stale_branches` tool. The server finds 14 branches untouched for 90+ days but has no idea if that threshold or that exact list is what the user actually wants.

Instead of deleting them or asking the model to re-prompt the user in chat, the server sends elicitation/create with a schema: a boolean `confirm` field and a number `days_threshold` field, plus a message listing the 14 branch names.

The client shows a real form. The user changes the threshold to 120 days and confirms — the server gets back `{action: "accept", content: {confirm: true, days_threshold: 120}}` and re-runs its own query with the corrected value, not a value the model invented.

slides.title: Elicitation vs. the Other MCP Primitives
bullets: Elicitation is the only primitive where the payload is a question for a human, not context for the model or a scope declaration.

rows: Server asks the human a direct, schema-shaped question
Server borrows the client's LLM to reason
Client tells server which directories are in scope
Model invokes a server function with args it already has

slides.title: The Restrictions Are the Point, Not a Limitation
bullets: The spec explicitly bans using elicitation to request sensitive information — passwords, API keys, credit card numbers have no business flowing through a form a server designed.

Flat-primitives-only isn't laziness: it keeps every client able to render a generic form without a bespoke UI per server, and stops elicitation from becoming a way to smuggle arbitrary structured data collection into a tool call.

Skip elicitation for anything the model can already infer from context, and for genuinely sensitive input — route those through the client's own auth flow instead. Reach for it when the missing piece is a fact, choice, or confirmation only the human has.

slides.title: A Form, Not a Chat Message
bullets: Elicitation gives a server a structured way to ask the human directly — mid-call — instead of failing, guessing, or offloading the question to the model.
Three response actions (accept / decline / cancel) preserve the difference between 'no' and 'not now,' which a server should handle differently.
Schemas are intentionally flat and primitive-only, and sensitive data is explicitly off-limits — the constraints exist to keep the channel safe and every client able to render it generically.

questions.prompt: What does a server send when it calls elicitation/create?
options: A raw text prompt for the model to answer on the user's behalf
A message plus a requestedSchema describing the structured input it needs
An OAuth token request
The full list of the client's declared roots
questions.explanation: elicitation/create carries a human-readable message and a requestedSchema (a restricted JSON Schema), which the client renders as a form for the human to fill in directly.

questions.prompt: Why does MCP elicitation use three response actions (accept, decline, cancel) instead of just success/failure?
options: To match HTTP status code conventions
Because decline (an explicit 'no') and cancel (dismissed without choosing) need different handling from a well-behaved server
It's a legacy artifact from an earlier protocol version
Because JSON-RPC requires exactly three response types
questions.explanation: A user explicitly declining is a real answer a server should respect; a user dismissing the dialog without choosing is inconclusive. Collapsing both into one 'failure' state would lose that distinction.

questions.prompt: Why are elicitation schemas restricted to flat objects with primitive properties only?
options: JSON Schema doesn't support nested objects at all
To keep every client able to render a generic form and to discourage using elicitation as a general-purpose data collection channel
Because nested schemas are too slow to parse
Because the MCP spec forbids servers from using enums
questions.explanation: Flat, primitive-only schemas mean any compliant client can render a sensible form without server-specific UI, and the constraint keeps elicitation scoped to quick, well-defined questions rather than arbitrary structured input.

posts.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration: Who Talks to Whom
posts.subtitle: Supervisor, pipeline, and swarm patterns — and the coordination tax each one charges.
posts.summary: Splitting a task across multiple LLM agents can cut context bloat and specialize behavior, but only if the coordination pattern fits the task. This post breaks down the three dominant multi-agent orchestration patterns — supervisor/worker, sequential pipeline, and decentralized swarm — with the concrete cost and failure tradeoffs of each.

slides.title: When One Agent Runs Out of Role
slides.body: A single agent juggling planning, coding, and reviewing tends to blur all three into mediocre output. Multi-agent orchestration splits the job across specialized agents — but the wiring between them decides whether that split helps or just multiplies cost.
bullets: Three dominant patterns: supervisor/worker, sequential pipeline, decentralized swarm
Every pattern trades coordination overhead for specialization
The wrong pattern for a simple task can cost 3-5x the tokens of one agent

slides.title: One Context Window, Too Many Jobs
slides.body: Stuff planning, tool use, self-critique, and long-term memory into one system prompt and each instruction competes for the model's attention.
bullets: A single agent's system prompt grows every time you add a responsibility
Role conflation: the same agent that wrote the code is asked to judge it, so it rarely catches its own mistakes
No natural checkpoint to inject human review or swap in a cheaper model for a simpler sub-step

slides.title: Split the Role, Not Just the Prompt
slides.body: Orchestration means one thing calls other agents like tools and decides what happens with what they return. The three shapes below differ in who holds that decision.
bullets: Supervisor/worker: one orchestrator agent routes each sub-task to a specialist and merges results
Sequential pipeline: fixed order, each agent's output is the next agent's entire input
Swarm (handoff): agents pass control directly to each other, no fixed center

slides.title: Three Shapes, Three Failure Modes
bullets: Supervisor/worker: a router agent picks the next specialist based on shared state — flexible, but the supervisor becomes a single point of failure and a bottleneck
Sequential pipeline: Planner -> Coder -> Reviewer -> Tester, each stage strictly gated on the last — predictable, but one bad handoff (a vague plan) poisons every stage after it
Swarm/handoff: any agent can transfer control to any other agent it knows about — cheap to add new agents, but nothing enforces that the whole thing terminates

slides.title: Worked Example: A Code-Review Agent Team
slides.body: A supervisor gets 'fix this failing test.' It doesn't fix anything itself — it only decides who acts next.
bullets: Supervisor reads the failure, calls a Diagnose agent with just the stack trace, not the whole repo
Diagnose agent returns a 3-line root-cause summary; supervisor passes that summary plus the one relevant file to a Patch agent
Patch agent proposes a diff; supervisor calls a Test agent to run it in a sandbox before ever showing the user
Total: 4 focused LLM calls with small contexts, versus 1 call carrying the entire repo diff, stack trace, and test output at once

slides.title: Picking a Pattern

rows: Dynamic routing when the right specialist isn't known in advance
Supervisor becomes the bottleneck and single point of failure
One bad stage output corrupts everything downstream
Open-ended tasks where the next best agent isn't fixed
No built-in termination check; can loop or hand off indefinitely

slides.title: The Coordination Tax
slides.body: Every extra agent hop is a full extra LLM call, and most of what it reads is a summary of what already happened, not new information.
bullets: N agents on one task means roughly N separate context windows and N latencies stacked, not parallel — cost and time both compound
Compounding error: if each agent stage is 90% reliable, a 4-stage sequential chain is only about 66% reliable end-to-end (0.9^4 ≈ 0.656)
Skip orchestration for tasks a single well-scoped prompt already handles well — the fix for a bad single-agent prompt is usually a better prompt, not more agents
Add a supervisor only once there are 3+ genuinely different specialist roles; two agents rarely need a third to referee them

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Multi-agent orchestration splits responsibility, it does not reduce total work — budget for roughly N times the tokens and latency of a single call
Supervisor/worker fits dynamic routing; sequential pipeline fits known multi-step processes; swarm fits open-ended handoffs
Compounding reliability is the hidden cost: chain enough 90%-reliable agents and the system-wide success rate drags below 70%
Default to one well-scoped agent; reach for orchestration only when there are genuinely distinct specialist roles that benefit from separate context

questions.prompt: In the supervisor/worker pattern, what is the supervisor's main job?
options: Executing every sub-task itself for consistency
Deciding which specialist agent handles the next step and merging results
Storing the long-term memory for all agents
Running the final unit tests
questions.explanation: The supervisor doesn't do the specialist work — it routes state to the right worker and decides what happens with what comes back. That routing role is also why it becomes the bottleneck: every decision passes through it.

questions.prompt: Why can a 4-stage sequential pipeline where each stage is 90% reliable end up below 70% reliable overall?
options: Because agents run out of context window
Because each stage's success is conditional on all previous stages succeeding, so probabilities multiply (0.9^4 ≈ 65.6%)
Because sequential pipelines always use a slower model
Because token limits force truncation after 3 agents
questions.explanation: Independent-stage reliabilities multiply in a strict sequential chain: 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 ≈ 0.656. A single bad handoff early in the chain poisons everything after it.

questions.prompt: A task can already be handled reliably by one well-scoped agent with a focused prompt. What's the right call?
options: Add a supervisor and two workers anyway, for future flexibility
Split it into a swarm so agents can hand off as needed
Keep it as one agent — orchestration adds cost and failure surface without a corresponding benefit here
Always use a sequential pipeline for consistency across the codebase
questions.explanation: Orchestration overhead — extra tokens, extra latency, compounding failure — is only worth paying when there are genuinely distinct specialist roles. A task one agent already handles well doesn't need more agents.

posts.title: Kimi K3: Moonshot's 2.8T Open-Weight Flagship
posts.subtitle: 896 experts, 16 fire per token, 1M-token context — and the full checkpoint is public.
posts.summary: Moonshot AI open-weighted Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model that activates only 104B parameters per token via 896 routed experts. It ships a native 1M-token context, a built-in MoonViT-V2 vision encoder, and MXFP4/MXFP8 quantization-aware weights — but serving the full checkpoint still needs a multi-GPU cluster.

slides.title: A 2.8-Trillion-Parameter Model, Fully Open
slides.body: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3's weights publicly — the largest open-weight model shipped to date, built as a sparse Mixture-of-Experts network rather than a dense giant.
bullets: 2.8T total parameters, only 104B activated per token
896 routed experts + 2 shared experts, 16 selected per token
Weights and code public under the Kimi K3 License

slides.title: Frontier-Tier Usually Means Closed-Weight
slides.body: The most capable models are almost all API-only. Open-weight releases have historically traded capability for openness.
bullets: Fable 5, Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.6 all ship as closed APIs, not downloadable weights
Prior open models stayed smaller to stay servable on modest hardware
A trillion-plus-parameter dense model would be too expensive to even run, let alone open-source

slides.title: Sparsity Is the Trick: 16 of 896 Experts Fire
slides.body: K3's Stable LatentMoE framework keeps almost all weights dormant on any given token, so compute scales with the 104B active slice, not the 2.8T total.
bullets: 93 layers total: 69 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers + 24 Gated Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) layers
Attention Residuals (AttnRes) stabilize training at this depth and sparsity
Native MXFP4 weights with MXFP8 activations via quantization-aware training, not post-hoc quantization

slides.title: One Encoder for Text, Image, and Video
slides.body: Multimodal input doesn't go through a bolted-on adapter — it's a native part of the model.
bullets: MoonViT-V2 vision encoder: 401M parameters, trained jointly with the language model
160K-token vocabulary
1,048,576-token context window (1M), enough for a large codebase or a long video transcript in one pass

slides.title: The Spec Sheet
What 1M Tokens Actually Buys You
slides.body: A concrete case: feeding K3 an entire mid-sized codebase plus its issue tracker history in one context window.
bullets: No manual chunking or retrieval step needed to fit the repo in context
The model can trace a bug across files it read directly, not summaries of files
Same context budget covers a multi-hour video transcript via the native vision/video path

slides.title: Open Weights ≠ Runs on a Laptop
slides.body: Sparsity cuts compute per token, not storage. The full 2.8T-parameter checkpoint still has to live somewhere.
bullets: Serving K3 needs vLLM, SGLang, or Moonshot's own TokenSpeed engine across multiple GPUs/nodes
Even MXFP4-quantized, a 2.8T-parameter checkpoint is a multi-hundred-gigabyte download and load
The 'Kimi K3 License' is Moonshot's own terms, not a standard OSI license — read it before commercial use
For most teams, the hosted API at platform.kimi.ai is the practical entry point, not self-hosting

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: 2.8T total / 104B active MoE, 896 experts with 16 selected per token — sparsity, not size, drives efficiency
1M-token context plus a native MoonViT-V2 encoder for text, image, and video in one model
Moonshot reports ~2.5× overall scaling efficiency versus Kimi K2
Weights are public, but serving the full checkpoint still needs multi-GPU infrastructure
License is custom ('Kimi K3 License') — check terms before commercial deployment

questions.prompt: How many of Kimi K3's 896 routed experts activate for a given token?
options: All 896
questions.explanation: 16 of 896 routed experts (plus 2 shared experts) fire per token. That sparsity is why only 104B of the 2.8T total parameters are activated per forward pass, cutting compute far below what a dense model of the same size would need.

questions.prompt: What lets Kimi K3 process images and video without a separate pipeline?
options: A bolt-on OCR plugin called after generation
The native MoonViT-V2 vision encoder trained as part of the model
Converting every image to a text caption before inference
It doesn't support images
questions.explanation: MoonViT-V2 (401M parameters) is built into K3 itself, so the model handles text, images, and video natively rather than routing through an external adapter.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't K3's open-weight release mean it can run on a single consumer GPU?
options: Because the license forbids local deployment
Because the full 2.8T-parameter checkpoint must still be stored and served, typically across multiple GPUs or nodes, even though only 104B parameters activate per token
Because it has no quantized version available
Because it only supports TPU hardware
questions.explanation: MoE sparsity reduces compute per token, not the memory needed to hold the model. Engines like vLLM and SGLang still have to load the entire 2.8T-parameter checkpoint — even in MXFP4 — across a multi-GPU cluster.

posts.title: GraphRAG: Retrieval Over a Graph, Not Just Chunks
posts.subtitle: When the question needs the shape of the whole dataset, nearest-neighbor chunks can't answer it.
posts.summary: GraphRAG extracts an LLM-generated knowledge graph from a corpus, clusters it into hierarchical communities, and pre-summarizes each one. That lets it answer whole-dataset questions ('what are the top themes here?') that plain vector RAG's nearest-neighbor chunk retrieval structurally can't reach — at the cost of a real upfront indexing pass.

slides.title: When Vector Search Can't See the Forest
slides.body: Standard RAG retrieves the chunks nearest to a query embedding. GraphRAG instead builds a knowledge graph from the corpus and reasons over its structure.
bullets: Built by Microsoft Research for questions that span an entire private dataset
Trades a real indexing cost for answers no single chunk contains
Open-sourced pipeline, 20K+ GitHub stars since its 2024 release

slides.title: 'Top 5 Themes' Isn't in Any One Chunk
slides.body: Top-k similarity search finds text that looks like the query — not text that summarizes the whole corpus.
bullets: Entity-focused queries ('What is Novorossiya?') work fine with plain vector RAG
Dataset-wide queries ('What are the top 5 themes in this dataset?') have no single matching chunk
Answering them requires aggregating across the entire corpus, which nearest-neighbor retrieval isn't built to do

slides.title: Extract a Graph, Then Summarize It Hierarchically
slides.body: GraphRAG's indexing pipeline runs once per corpus, before any query arrives.
bullets: 1. An LLM reads every chunk and extracts entities and relationships into a graph
2. The graph is broken into hierarchical communities via bottom-up clustering (Microsoft's graspologic library)
3. An LLM pre-generates a summary for every community, at every level of the hierarchy
4. At query time, the question is routed to global or local search over these pre-built structures

slides.title: Global Search vs. Local (DRIFT) Search
slides.body: The two query types hit completely different parts of the index.
bullets: Global search: map-reduce over community summaries — for holistic questions like 'catch me up on the last two weeks'
Local/DRIFT search: walks the entity neighborhood around specific nodes — for precise, entity-focused questions
Picking the wrong mode either wastes tokens scanning irrelevant summaries or misses the aggregate answer entirely

slides.title: Dynamic Community Selection: Real Numbers
slides.body: Microsoft Research measured what pruning irrelevant communities before the expensive map-reduce step actually costs and buys.

rows: +34% cost, but 58.8%/60.0% win rate on comprehensiveness/empowerment

slides.title: A Support Ticket Corpus, Two Ways
slides.body: Query: "What are the top recurring themes in last quarter's tickets?"
bullets: Vector RAG: returns a handful of tickets whose embeddings are closest to the query — none of them individually describes an aggregate theme
GraphRAG: entities like 'login flow', 'billing', 'mobile crash' were already extracted and clustered into a 'product areas' community during indexing
The LLM answers by combining a few pre-written community summaries instead of skimming thousands of raw tickets

slides.title: Tradeoffs and Takeaways
slides.body: The indexing pass is the real cost: an LLM call per chunk to extract entities, then more calls to summarize every community at every level — paid upfront, unlike vector RAG's cheap one-time embedding step.
bullets: Worth it for corpora queried repeatedly where dataset-wide questions matter (research libraries, internal wikis) — overkill for a single-document Q&A bot
Graph quality depends entirely on how well the LLM extracts entities; bad extraction means a bad graph
Dynamic community selection cut global-search token cost 77% with no quality loss at shallow depth (Microsoft Research)
GraphRAG complements local/vector search via DRIFT mode — it doesn't replace it

questions.prompt: Why does plain vector RAG struggle with a question like 'what are the top 5 themes in this dataset'?
options: Embeddings can't be computed for long documents
No single chunk contains an aggregate answer across the whole corpus — nearest-neighbor retrieval only finds locally similar text
Vector databases can't store more than a few thousand chunks
LLMs can't read more than one retrieved chunk at a time
questions.explanation: Top-k similarity search finds chunks that look like the query, not chunks that summarize the whole dataset. Global questions need aggregation across the corpus, which is exactly what GraphRAG's pre-built community summaries provide.

questions.prompt: In GraphRAG, what does a 'community' represent?
options: A single source document
A cluster of related entities in the extracted knowledge graph, grouped hierarchically
A group of users who asked similar questions
A shard of the vector index
questions.explanation: After extracting entities and relationships into a graph, GraphRAG runs bottom-up clustering to group related entities into communities at multiple hierarchy levels, then pre-summarizes each one.

questions.prompt: Per Microsoft Research's measurements, what did dynamic community selection achieve at search-depth level 1 versus static global search?
options: 34% higher cost for better quality
77% lower token cost with no drop in quality
A completely different knowledge graph structure
No measurable difference in cost or quality
questions.explanation: By rating community relevance top-down and pruning irrelevant branches before the expensive map-reduce step, dynamic selection cut community reports processed from ~1,500 to ~470 — a 77% token-cost reduction — while matching static search's quality at that depth.

posts.title: Self-Consistency: Voting Across Multiple Reasoning Paths
posts.subtitle: Why sampling several chains of thought beats trusting just one
posts.summary: Self-consistency samples several independent chains of thought at nonzero temperature and takes the majority final answer instead of trusting one greedy path. It needs no extra training or verifier model, but costs k times the inference compute and only works when answers can be compared.

slides.title: Self-Consistency: Voting Across Multiple Reasoning Paths
slides.body: One chain of thought is one roll of the dice. Self-consistency rolls it many times and lets the crowd decide.

slides.title: A Single Greedy Chain of Thought Is a Coin Flip
slides.body: Standard chain-of-thought prompting generates one reasoning path and reads off its final answer. On multi-step problems, a single wrong turn early in the chain — a dropped term, a misread number — quietly cascades into a confidently wrong final answer.
bullets: Greedy decoding always picks the same tokens, so one bad early step is never corrected
The model can't tell you how confident it actually is — it just states the answer
Longer reasoning chains have more steps where a single slip derails everything

slides.title: Sample Many Paths, Then Take the Majority Answer
slides.body: Instead of decoding one chain greedily, sample k independent chains of thought at temperature > 0, extract each path's final answer, and return whichever answer appears most often.
bullets: No fine-tuning, no reward model, no verifier — pure inference-time technique
Each sample explores a different route through the reasoning space
The final answer is a vote across paths, not a single model's single guess

slides.title: Why Wrong Paths Don't Agree With Each Other
slides.body: Correct reasoning tends to converge: different valid routes through a problem usually land on the same answer. Errors are different — a dropped term here, a sign flip there — and they scatter across many different wrong answers instead of clustering on one.
bullets: Agreement across independently-sampled paths is used as a proxy for correctness
It behaves like an ensemble vote, but from one model sampled repeatedly, not many models
More samples make the correct cluster easier to separate from scattered noise

slides.title: One Word Problem, Five Sampled Paths
slides.body: A model is asked a multi-step arithmetic word problem. Sampled five times at temperature 0.7, four paths reason through the steps differently but all land on 42; one path drops a term midway and lands on 39.
bullets: Path A, B, C, D: different phrasing of the reasoning, same final answer — 42
Path E: skips a subtraction step, final answer — 39
Majority vote: 42 wins 4-to-1, and that's the answer returned
A single greedy decode might have been path E — self-consistency would have caught it

slides.title: Greedy vs. Beam Search vs. Self-Consistency
slides.body: The three sit on a spectrum from cheap-and-brittle to expensive-and-robust.

rows: Still converges on one dominant path
k independent samples, majority vote on final answer
Needs answers that can be compared, e.g. a number or letter

slides.title: The Catch: k Times the Compute, and a Checkable Answer
slides.body: Self-consistency isn't free. Its cost and its requirements both come from the same source: you need k full generations, and you need a clean way to compare their outputs.
bullets: Cost scales linearly with the number of samples — commonly tens of samples per question
Latency multiplies unless the samples are run in parallel
Only works when final answers are extractable and comparable: a number, a label, a short span
Doesn't help open-ended generation — essays or stories have no single answer to vote on
Returns diminish after enough samples; doubling k rarely doubles the accuracy gain

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Self-consistency is an inference-time-only technique: sample k chains of thought, marginalize by majority vote
It works because correct reasoning converges while errors scatter across different wrong answers
Strongest on structured reasoning with a checkable final answer: math, logic, multiple-choice QA
Costs roughly k times the compute of a single generation — budget for it accordingly
A foundational building block behind later test-time-compute and search-based reasoning methods

questions.prompt: What does self-consistency add on top of standard chain-of-thought prompting?
options: Fine-tuning on multiple reasoning traces
Sampling several independent reasoning paths and majority-voting the final answers
Replacing the LLM with a symbolic search algorithm
A separate reward model that scores each reasoning path
questions.explanation: Self-consistency is purely an inference-time sampling-and-voting scheme — no extra training and no separate verifier or reward model. That's what makes it a cheap add-on rather than a new system.

questions.prompt: Why does majority voting tend to recover the correct answer even when some sampled paths are wrong?
options: Wrong reasoning paths are systematically biased toward the same incorrect answer
The model is fine-tuned to know which paths are correct
Correct reasoning tends to converge on the same answer via different routes, while independent errors scatter across different wrong answers
Temperature is set to 0 so every sampled path is identical
questions.explanation: Valid reasoning chains tend to reach the same destination by different routes, while mistakes are essentially independent noise that lands on different wrong answers — so agreement is evidence of correctness.

questions.prompt: Self-consistency is a poor fit for which of these tasks?
options: Grade-school math word problems
Multiple-choice commonsense reasoning
Open-ended essay or creative-writing generation with no single checkable answer
Multi-step logic puzzles
questions.explanation: Majority voting needs a way to compare final answers. Free-form generation has no clean equivalence check between samples, so there's nothing to vote on.

posts.title: Reflection: An Agent That Critiques Its Own Output
posts.subtitle: A checkpoint between act and observe: score the last output, then decide whether to redo it.
posts.summary: Reflection adds a critique-then-revise checkpoint to an agent loop: after producing an attempt, an evaluator — ideally grounded in something external like tests or retrieval — scores it and the actor revises before moving on. It's the difference between a plain act-observe cycle and a loop that can catch and fix its own mistakes, at the cost of extra latency and the risk of an ungrounded self-judgment looping forever.

slides.title: An Agent That Critiques Its Own Output
slides.body: Most agent loops act, then move on. A reflection loop adds one more step: before continuing, the agent scores its own last output and decides whether to redo it.
bullets: Popularized by patterns like Reflexion and Self-Refine, now a standard layer in coding and research agents
Turns the agent into its own reviewer between 'act' and 'observe'
Costs extra latency and tokens — it's not free, and it's not always worth it

slides.title: A Wrong First Draft Just Becomes the Final Answer
slides.body: Single-pass generation, and even a plain reasoning-and-tool-calling loop, have no built-in mechanism for the agent to say 'this is wrong, try again' unless the environment itself signals failure.
bullets: An LLM asked to write code, summarize a doc, or answer a question usually stops at its first draft
Interleaving reasoning and tool calls doesn't force the agent to grade what it just produced
Errors compound silently: a flawed step 2 output feeds straight into step 3 with no checkpoint in between

slides.title: Actor, Then Critic, Then Revise
slides.body: A reflection loop wraps generation in three roles — which can be the same model prompted differently, or two separate models entirely.
bullets: Actor produces an attempt: an answer, a function, a plan step
Evaluator scores the attempt and states what's wrong — a self-critique prompt, unit tests, a compiler, or a separate judge model
Actor revises using that critique as new context, and the loop repeats until a pass signal or a max-iteration cap is hit

slides.title: Grounded Feedback Beats the Model Judging Itself
slides.body: The biggest lever in how well reflection works is where the critique comes from.
bullets: Grounded: unit test results, a compiler error, a retrieved fact, a calculator output — feedback the model can't talk its way around
Ungrounded: the same model re-reading its own output and guessing whether it's correct
The Reflexion-style pattern works best when the critique is anchored to an external signal, not pure self-judgment — a model that made a mistake can miss the same mistake on review

slides.title: A Coding Agent Reflecting on a Failing Test
slides.body: A concrete walkthrough of one reflection round.
bullets: Actor writes a function to parse a date string and submits it
Evaluator runs the test suite: 2 of 5 cases fail, including one with a two-digit year
The failure trace — not a vague 'looks fine to me' — becomes the critique; the actor patches the year-parsing branch and resubmits
Evaluator reruns the same suite: 5 of 5 pass, loop exits on the grounded pass signal

slides.title: Reflection vs. Plain Tool-Use Loops vs. Tree Search

rows: Interleaved reasoning + tool calls, no self-grading step
Explores multiple candidate paths, backtracks on dead ends
An explicit critique-then-revise checkpoint after an attempt

slides.title: When Reflection Backfires
bullets: Ungrounded self-critique can rubber-stamp its own mistakes — same model, same blind spots, now with false confidence
Without a max-iteration cap, a stuck agent can loop indefinitely, revising a wrong answer into a different wrong answer
Every extra round roughly doubles the tokens and latency for that step — fine for a one-shot code fix, wasteful for a low-latency chat reply
Skip it for trivial tasks, when there's nothing to ground the critique in, or when the latency budget can't absorb another round-trip

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: Reflection = act, then critique, then revise — a checkpoint plain generation and simple tool-use loops don't have
Ground the critique in something external (tests, retrieval, a rubric) whenever possible; pure self-judgment is the weakest version
Always cap iterations — an ungrounded reflection loop has no guarantee it ever converges

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between a plain act-observe agent loop and a reflection loop?
options: Reflection never uses tools
Reflection adds an explicit critique-and-revise checkpoint after an attempt, which the plain loop doesn't have
Reflection only works for code generation
The plain loop requires a separate judge model and reflection never does
questions.explanation: A plain act-observe loop interleaves reasoning and tool calls but has no built-in step where the agent grades its own output before moving on. Reflection inserts exactly that checkpoint: attempt, critique, revise.

questions.prompt: Why is grounded feedback (like test results or a compiler error) generally more reliable than a model critiquing its own output?
options: Grounded feedback is always free to compute
An ungrounded self-critique shares the same blind spots as the generation that produced the mistake
Grounded feedback requires no extra latency
Models are architecturally incapable of generating self-critiques
questions.explanation: When the same model that made a mistake is also asked to judge it, it can miss the exact same thing twice. An external, grounded signal — a failing test, a retrieved fact — doesn't share that blind spot.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of running a reflection loop with no maximum iteration cap?
options: It runs too fast to produce useful output
It can loop indefinitely, revising a wrong answer into a different wrong answer without ever converging
It always stops after exactly one revision automatically
It bypasses the actor role entirely
questions.explanation: Without a stop condition, an ungrounded or poorly-grounded reflection loop has no guarantee of convergence — it can keep 'fixing' an answer in circles. A max-iteration cap or a hard pass/fail signal is what actually bounds it.

posts.title: DPO: Skipping the Reward Model Entirely
posts.subtitle: Turning a preference pair directly into a loss function — no reward model, no PPO rollouts.
posts.summary: Direct Preference Optimization reframes RLHF as a single supervised classification loss: given a chosen and rejected response to the same prompt, it directly increases the model's relative log-probability of the chosen one. It proves that this loss has the exact same optimal policy as the RL objective PPO is trying to solve — RLHF's math, without RLHF's machinery. The tradeoff is that DPO fits a fixed, offline preference dataset, while PPO-based RLHF can keep sampling and re-ranking new completions as the policy shifts.

slides.title: One Loss Function, No Reward Model
slides.body: RLHF normally needs three models in memory at once: policy, reward model, and a frozen reference copy, coordinated through PPO. DPO collapses that into one classification-style loss on preference pairs.
bullets: Introduced in 2023 (Rafailov et al., Stanford) as a drop-in replacement for the RL stage of RLHF
Trains directly on (prompt, chosen response, rejected response) triples
No reward model to train, no rollouts to sample, no PPO hyperparameters to tune

slides.title: Classic RLHF Is a Three-Stage Rube Goldberg Machine
slides.body: Standard RLHF trains a reward model on human preference pairs, then runs PPO to optimize the policy against that reward model, all while a KL penalty holds it near a frozen reference model.
bullets: Stage 1: train a reward model r(x,y) on labeled (chosen, rejected) pairs
Stage 2: run PPO — sample completions, score them with r, update the policy, repeat for thousands of steps
PPO is notoriously finicky: reward hacking, value-function instability, and sensitive hyperparameters make it hard to reproduce

slides.title: The Reward Model Has a Closed-Form Solution
slides.body: The key insight: for a KL-constrained reward maximization objective, the optimal policy can be written analytically in terms of the reward function. Invert that relationship and the reward function drops out of the training loss entirely.
bullets: The RLHF objective's optimal policy has a known closed form: it's the reference policy re-weighted by exp(reward / beta)
Solving that equation for the reward turns it into a function of the policy itself, not a separate network
Substituting that back into the standard Bradley-Terry preference loss gives a loss written purely in terms of policy log-probabilities

slides.title: The DPO Loss, in Plain Terms
slides.body: For each pair, DPO compares how much the policy's log-probability of the chosen response has grown relative to the reference model, versus how much the rejected response's has grown.
bullets: loss = -log sigmoid( beta * [ (logP_policy(chosen) - logP_ref(chosen)) - (logP_policy(rejected) - logP_ref(rejected)) ] )
beta controls how far the policy is allowed to drift from the frozen reference model — small beta means aggressive updates
The reference model's log-probs are computed once and cached; only the policy model needs gradient updates

slides.title: Worked Example: One Preference Pair
slides.body: Prompt: 'Explain recursion.' Chosen: a clear explanation with a base case. Rejected: a vague, circular non-answer.
bullets: Suppose the policy already assigns the chosen response a higher log-prob than the reference model does (+2.1 nats), and the rejected response a lower one (-0.4 nats)
The margin (+2.1) - (-0.4) = 2.5 is scaled by beta (e.g. 0.1) and passed through -log(sigmoid(x))
A positive, growing margin drives the loss toward zero; the gradient step nudges the model to further favor the chosen response and suppress the rejected one, in that single backward pass

slides.title: DPO vs. PPO-Based RLHF

rows: Online — samples new completions each step
Sensitive to reward hacking, value-loss collapse
Standard supervised-style training, far more stable
Can improve past the dataset's ceiling
Yes — reward model generalizes to new samples
Bounded by what the static pairs teach it

slides.title: Where DPO Falls Short
slides.body: Removing the reward model removes a source of instability, but also removes a capability: PPO's reward model can score completions the policy hasn't seen yet, which is exactly how online RL keeps improving past its seed data.
bullets: DPO can overfit to the specific chosen/rejected pairs it was given, especially with a small or noisy preference dataset
Because the loss only looks at relative log-probs, a policy can 'win' by pushing rejected-response probability toward zero rather than actually improving the chosen response
For domains where preferences shift as the policy improves (e.g. iterative red-teaming), online RL methods still have an edge — DPO needs a fresh round of pairs to catch up

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: DPO proves the RLHF reward-then-PPO pipeline has a hidden closed form — you can optimize the same objective with one supervised-style loss on preference pairs
beta is the one knob that matters: it sets how far the policy can drift from the reference model per pair
Reach for DPO when you have a solid static preference dataset and want RLHF-grade alignment without PPO's instability; reach for online RL when the policy needs to keep improving past that dataset

questions.prompt: What does DPO eliminate from the standard RLHF pipeline?
options: The frozen reference model
The separate reward model and the PPO sampling loop
The need for any human preference labels
The KL penalty entirely
questions.explanation: DPO still uses a frozen reference model and still relies on human (or AI) preference labels — it just proves the reward model and PPO's online sampling loop are unnecessary, because the optimal policy has a closed-form relationship to the reward that lets you substitute it directly into the loss.

questions.prompt: In the DPO loss, what does the beta parameter control?
options: The learning rate of the optimizer
How many preference pairs are used per batch
How far the policy is allowed to drift from the reference model
The temperature used during inference sampling
questions.explanation: Beta scales the margin between chosen and rejected log-probability ratios inside the loss. A smaller beta permits larger deviations from the reference model per update; a larger beta keeps the policy closer to its starting point.

questions.prompt: Why might PPO-based RLHF still outperform DPO in some settings?
options: PPO doesn't require any human labels at all
PPO's reward model can score newly sampled completions, letting the policy keep improving past its original dataset
PPO is simpler to implement and more stable to train
DPO cannot be used with a KL penalty
questions.explanation: Because PPO samples fresh completions and scores them with a learned reward model, it can keep discovering and reinforcing better behavior online. DPO trains on a fixed, offline set of pairs, so it's bounded by what those pairs teach it — it can't generalize a reward signal to responses it never saw labeled.

posts.title: MCP Prompts: Templates the User Invokes, Not the Model
posts.subtitle: The one MCP primitive where a human, not the LLM, decides when it fires.
posts.summary: MCP defines three server primitives with three different controllers: tools the model calls, resources the app attaches, and prompts the user explicitly fires. A prompt is a reusable template — the client calls prompts/list to see what's available and prompts/get with arguments to receive the fully rendered messages ready to send to the model. It's the primitive built for standardizing a team's best workflows, but it's also the least consistently supported across MCP clients.

slides.title: The Prompt the User Picks, Not the Model
slides.body: MCP defines three server primitives. Tools are for the model. Resources are for the app. Prompts are the one built for a human to trigger on purpose.
bullets: Surfaces as a slash-command or menu item in the client, not a free-form message
Turns a team's best prompt into something everyone invokes the same way
Part of the same spec that defines Tools, Resources, Sampling, Roots, and Elicitation

slides.title: Free-Form Prompts Don't Scale Across a Team
slides.body: Ad hoc prompting means ten engineers write ten slightly different versions of 'review this PR,' each missing different context.
bullets: Tools solve 'let the model decide what to call' — they don't solve 'let the user reliably trigger a known-good workflow'
Copy-pasting a prompt template from a wiki page breaks the moment the underlying schema changes
MCP Prompts let the server own the template and version it once, for every client that connects

slides.title: Three Primitives, Three Different Controllers
slides.body: The MCP spec splits control deliberately around one question: who decides when something runs.
bullets: Tools — model-controlled: the LLM decides to call one based on the conversation
Resources — app-controlled: the client attaches data automatically as context
Prompts — user-controlled: a human explicitly selects and fires one from the UI

slides.title: Two Calls: List, Then Get
slides.body: prompts/list returns each prompt's name, description, and typed arguments. prompts/get is called with a name plus argument values and returns the fully rendered messages.
bullets: Each argument can be marked required, so the client can build a form before firing the request
The rendered result is a list of role-tagged messages — the same shape a chat completion expects
A message can embed a resource directly, so one prompt call can package instructions plus a document in one shot

slides.title: A Slash Command for Reviewing a Diff
slides.body: A code-review MCP server exposes a prompt named review-diff with one required argument: diff.
bullets: In a client with prompts support it shows up as a pickable slash command in the message composer
The user selects it, pastes the diff into the argument field, and the client fires the request
prompts/get returns a fully-formed message: the team's actual review checklist plus the diff, identical for every engineer who runs it

slides.title: Prompts vs. Tools vs. Resources

rows: Look up data, take an action, call an API
Attach a file, a database row, a config as context
Fire a known-good, reusable workflow template

slides.title: Where Prompts Fall Short
slides.body: Prompts are the least uniformly supported MCP primitive — check before you rely on them.
bullets: Not every MCP client renders a prompts picker UI; a server that only ships prompts (no tools) may be invisible in some clients
Static by default — if the available set changes, the server must send a prompts/list_changed notification or the client's UI goes stale
Overloading a prompt with many optional arguments turns a one-click workflow back into a form the user has to fill out by hand

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: Prompts are the MCP primitive a human fires on purpose — not the model, not the client automatically
List then get: list the templates and their typed arguments, then get the fully rendered messages for one call
Use prompts for the workflow you want every user to run identically — not for anything the model should decide on its own

questions.prompt: In the Model Context Protocol, which primitive is explicitly meant to be triggered by the user, not the model?
options: Tools
Resources
Prompts
Sampling
questions.explanation: Tools are model-controlled and resources are typically attached automatically by the client; prompts are the primitive designed for a human to select and fire on purpose, often surfaced as a slash command.

questions.prompt: What two protocol calls does a client use to work with a server's prompts?
options: prompts/list and prompts/get
prompts/create and prompts/delete
prompts/render and prompts/submit
prompts/fetch and prompts/run
questions.explanation: prompts/list returns the available templates with their name, description, and typed arguments; prompts/get is called with argument values and returns the fully rendered messages ready to send to the model.

questions.prompt: Why might a well-built MCP prompt still never appear to a user?
options: Prompts require a paid API tier
The connecting client may not implement a UI for browsing or invoking prompts
Prompts can only be used with resources attached
The server must be restarted before every prompt call
questions.explanation: Client support for the prompts primitive isn't universal — a client without a prompts picker simply won't surface prompts a server exposes, even though the same server's tools work fine.

posts.title: Spark-to-Paper: An AI That Runs Its Own Research Loop
posts.subtitle: Thirteen composable skills turn a raw idea into a submittable paper, end to end.
posts.summary: Spark-to-Paper (arXiv:2608.11924) implements end-to-end research paper generation as thirteen composable skills inside an existing coding assistant. It separates deterministic checks from model judgment and specifies evidence requirements before experiments run, then bounds a documented failure mode called the Self-Refutation Loop where iterative self-critique talks the model out of correct findings.

slides.title: Can an AI Run Its Own Research Loop?
slides.body: A new system turns a one-line research idea into a full paper draft, without a bespoke agent platform.
bullets: Thirteen composable skills
Runs inside an existing coding assistant
Posted to arXiv Aug 12, 2026

slides.title: Writing a Paper Is Not One Task, It's Ten
slides.body: Turning an idea into a paper means retrieving literature, designing and running experiments, revising claims to match evidence, producing figures, and staying consistent across a long generation process — all before a word of the final draft is 'done'.
bullets: A single long LLM call collapses these into one blob and drifts
Claims and figures easily go out of sync with what was actually measured
Long generation runs compound small errors into large ones

slides.title: Thirteen Skills, Not One Giant Agent
slides.body: Spark-to-Paper is implemented as thirteen composable skills inside an existing coding assistant — no separate orchestration platform required.
bullets: Deterministic, checkable operations (retrieval, running code, checking a figure against its data) are split from model judgment calls
Experiment planning is separated from reporting: success criteria are written down before results are observed
That ordering is the whole trick — it blocks after-the-fact rationalization of whatever the experiment happened to produce

slides.title: The Self-Refutation Loop
slides.body: A documented failure mode: when a model repeatedly critiques its own claims, it can spiral — talking itself out of a correct finding, or into an incorrect one, on each pass.
bullets: Self-critique alone doesn't converge to truth, it converges to whatever the last critique argued
Spark-to-Paper bounds the loop with deterministic integrity checks that anchor revisions back to measured evidence
Bounding it isn't eliminating it — see the pitfalls slide

slides.title: From a One-Line Hypothesis to a Draft Section
slides.body: A researcher inputs: 'Does the order of examples in a prompt affect retrieval accuracy?' The system doesn't just answer — it works the loop.
bullets: Retrieval skill pulls related prior work before any experiment is designed
Planning skill locks in a success metric and a threshold up front
Execution skill runs the actual test and logs raw output
Reporting skill revises the claim to match what was measured — not what was hoped for — then generates the figure from the same run

slides.title: Who Owns Each Step

rows: Judging whether evidence supports a claim
Checking a figure matches its underlying data
Revising the narrative to fit results
Model judgment, bounded by the anti-refutation checks

slides.title: Where This Breaks
slides.body: This is scaffolding for the writing-and-evidencing loop, not a substitute for a good research question.
bullets: Inherits the limits of the underlying coding assistant it runs inside (context handling, tool errors)
The Self-Refutation Loop is bounded, not solved — it's a named risk to watch for, not a guarantee
A weak or trivial starting hypothesis still produces a weak paper, just a fluently-written one
Doesn't replace peer review or domain expertise on whether the question was worth asking

slides.title: The Real Insight Isn't 'AI Writes Papers'
slides.body: It's the ordering discipline: decide what would count as evidence before you see the results, and keep deterministic checks between the model and its own claims.
bullets: Separate what can be checked by code from what needs judgment
Lock success criteria in before running the experiment
Bound self-critique loops instead of trusting them to converge on their own

questions.prompt: What does the 'Self-Refutation Loop' describe in Spark-to-Paper?
options: A security exploit where the agent leaks training data
A failure mode where repeated self-critique spirals the model away from a correct finding
A reinforcement learning training algorithm
A formatting bug in generated LaTeX
questions.explanation: It's a named failure mode of iterative self-critique: without an anchor, each critique pass can push the model further from — not closer to — the correct claim. Spark-to-Paper bounds it with deterministic integrity checks.

questions.prompt: Why does the system lock in success criteria before running an experiment?
options: To make the experiment run faster
It's an arXiv submission requirement
To prevent revising the claim after seeing results — i.e. cherry-picking or rationalizing
To reduce the number of API calls needed
questions.explanation: Committing to what counts as evidence before observing outcomes is the core discipline: it blocks the common failure of quietly reshaping a claim to fit whatever result actually came out.

questions.prompt: How is Spark-to-Paper architected?
options: As a standalone multi-agent orchestration platform
As a single fine-tuned model checkpoint
As thirteen composable skills running inside an existing coding assistant
As a browser extension for Google Docs
questions.explanation: No bespoke agent platform — the thirteen skills are composable pieces that plug into a coding assistant that already exists, which is part of why the approach is notable.

references.title: Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill (arXiv:2608.11924)

posts.title: Grok 4.6: SpaceXAI's First Flagship After the Merger
posts.subtitle: xAI is gone — fully absorbed into SpaceX — and its first post-merger model trades raw IQ for agentic stamina.
posts.summary: SpaceXAI (the rebrand of xAI after its full merger into SpaceX) shipped Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, just 35 days after Grok 4.5. It scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — matching GPT-5.6 Sol — and is tuned for long-running agentic work: it finishes long knowledge-work tasks in about half the turns Claude Opus 5 needs, at $0.84 per task, though it still trails Opus 5 on raw agentic Elo.

slides.title: Grok Just Got a New Parent Company
slides.body: The first flagship model released since xAI was fully folded into SpaceX and renamed SpaceXAI.
bullets: Released August 12, 2026
35 days after Grok 4.5
Tuned for long-running agents, not a ground-up rebuild

slides.title: Why the Rebrand Is Part of the Story
slides.body: This isn't a naming gimmick — it's a real corporate restructuring that changes who ships and supports Grok going forward.
bullets: SpaceX acquired xAI in an all-stock deal in February 2026
xAI was dissolved as a standalone company and fully integrated into SpaceX by July 2026
Grok models, the X platform, and related AI infrastructure now sit under the SpaceXAI umbrella inside SpaceX

slides.title: What Actually Changed in 4.6
slides.body: The architecture didn't get a ground-up rewrite — the training recipe and target use case did.
bullets: Context window unchanged from Grok 4.5: 500,000 tokens
Training added a longer supplemental run using Grok-4.5-regenerated SFT trajectories, filtered by model-based checks
Followed by agentic reinforcement learning targeted at long-running agent tasks and interactive/visual work

slides.title: The Numbers

rows: 61 — up 5 points from Grok 4.5, matches GPT-5.6 Sol, one point behind Claude Fable 5
Elo 1577 on debut — behind Claude Opus 5
~53 turns to finish a task vs. Opus 5's ~103, at $0.84/task

slides.title: A Long-Horizon Task, Turn by Turn
slides.body: AA-Briefcase scores agents on real long-horizon knowledge-work projects — the kind that take dozens of tool calls, not a single prompt-response.
bullets: Grok 4.6 wraps the same class of task in roughly half the turns Claude Opus 5 needs
At $0.84 per completed task, it's built to be cheap to run at that pace
But Opus 5 still finishes with a higher completion-quality Elo — Grok 4.6 is faster and cheaper, not (yet) better on this benchmark

slides.title: Fast and Cheap Isn't the Same as Ahead
slides.body: Read the benchmarks as a tradeoff, not a crown.
bullets: Matches GPT-5.6 Sol on raw intelligence, trails Claude Fable 5 by a point — not the outright smartest model on the board
Wins on cost and turn-efficiency for agentic work, not on peak agentic quality where Opus 5 still leads
A 35-day release cadence plus a same-quarter full corporate absorption into SpaceX is fast — worth watching whether safety review depth keeps pace with release speed

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: xAI no longer exists as a standalone company — it's SpaceXAI, fully inside SpaceX
Grok 4.6 ties GPT-5.6 Sol on raw intelligence and is priced/tuned for long agentic runs
It's the efficiency pick for long-horizon agent tasks, not the peak-quality pick — that's still Claude Opus 5 by this benchmark

posts.title: Context Rot: Why Bigger Windows Don't Mean Better Recall
posts.subtitle: Every frontier model tested degrades as input grows, often well before it hits the documented limit.
posts.summary: Context rot is the well-documented tendency of LLMs to answer less reliably as input length grows, even far short of their advertised context limit. Chroma's 2025 study found this in all 18 frontier models tested, and earlier work ('Lost in the Middle') showed accuracy drops over 30% when a key fact sits mid-prompt instead of at the start or end. Counterintuitively, well-structured input can degrade attention more than shuffled input. The practical fix is retrieving a narrow, relevant slice of context rather than trusting a large window to hold everything reliably.

slides.title: The Context Window Lied to You
slides.body: A 200K-token window doesn't mean 200K tokens of reliable recall.
bullets: 18 frontier models tested, all degrade
Serious accuracy loss can appear at just 25% of the stated limit
Chroma Research, July 2025

slides.title: More Tokens, Worse Answers
slides.body: 'Context rot' names a specific finding: accuracy drops non-uniformly as input length grows — present at every length increment tested, in every model tested.
bullets: Contradicts the assumption that a bigger window means it's safe to just paste everything in
A 200K-token window can show serious accuracy loss with only ~50K tokens of actual input
GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4, and Gemini 2.5 were among the models exhibiting it

slides.title: Lost in the Middle
slides.body: Liu et al. (TACL 2024) found a U-shaped position effect on multi-document QA and key-value retrieval tasks.
bullets: Accuracy is highest when the relevant fact sits at the very start or end of the prompt
Accuracy drops by more than 30% when that same fact is buried in the middle
Replicated across six model families: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, Claude 1.3, LongChat-13B, MPT-30B, Cohere Command

slides.title: The Counterintuitive Part
slides.body: You'd expect well-organized, coherent input to help a model find what it needs. Chroma found the opposite at scale.
bullets: Coherent, well-structured input degraded attention MORE than shuffled, incoherent input
Structure that helps a human reader doesn't reliably help a transformer's attention over long context
It's a reminder that human reading intuitions don't automatically transfer to how these models actually attend

slides.title: Debugging a 90K-Token System Prompt
slides.body: An engineer stuffs a 90K-token onboarding doc plus tool specs into a system prompt, with the one critical safety instruction placed in the middle.
bullets: The agent silently ignores that instruction on a meaningful fraction of runs
Not because the instruction is wrong — because of where it sits in the prompt
Moving the same instruction to the very start (or repeating it at the end) measurably improves adherence

slides.title: Where Accuracy Actually Holds

headers: What Chroma / Liu et al. Observed
rows: Input well under the stated context limit
Input around ~25% of the stated window (e.g. 50K of 200K)
Serious accuracy loss can already appear
Key fact placed in the middle vs. start/end
Accuracy drops over 30% (Lost in the Middle)
Structured input can degrade attention more, not less

slides.title: So What Do You Actually Do?
slides.body: Treat a large context window as capacity, not as a guarantee of recall.
bullets: Don't paste an entire corpus just because the window fits it — retrieve the relevant 50K-200K tokens first, then reason over that
Put the most critical instruction at the very start or end of a long prompt, never buried in the middle
Test your prompts at the lengths you'll actually run in production, not just at the documented maximum

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: Context rot is universal across frontier models, not a quirk of one lab's model
Position matters as much as presence — start/end beats middle by a wide margin
Retrieval-then-reason beats dump-everything-in-the-window, even when the window technically fits it all

questions.explanation: The degradation showed up in all 18 frontier models tested, at every input-length increment — including well-known models like GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4, and Gemini 2.5.

At the very start or end of the context
It doesn't matter
Split evenly throughout the prompt
questions.explanation: Liu et al. found a U-shaped curve: accuracy is highest when key information sits at the start or end, and drops over 30% when it's buried in the middle.

questions.explanation: Chroma found structured input can hurt long-context attention more than shuffled input — a case where human-reading intuition doesn't predict model behavior.

posts.title: Test-Time Capability Transfer: Harnesses, Not Fine-Tuning
posts.subtitle: A stronger model writes deterministic scaffolding that nearly doubles a weaker model's accuracy — no gradient update in sight.
posts.summary: Salesforce AI Research and UIUC show that a strong 'builder' model can write a deterministic inference-time harness — code, routing, and format rules — that lets a much weaker 'target' model solve tasks it otherwise fails, without touching a single weight. On four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks, average target accuracy went from 0.49 to 0.91.

slides.title: One Model Builds the Harness, Another Runs It
slides.body: AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses — Salesforce AI Research + UIUC, arXiv:2608.12307, Aug 12 2026.
bullets: No fine-tuning, no distillation, no new weights
Capability moves through scaffolding, not parameters

slides.title: Weak Models Don't Fail Randomly — They Fail Predictably
slides.body: A small or cheap model missing a benchmark usually isn't 'less intelligent' in a fuzzy sense — it mis-formats answers, skips reasoning steps, or picks the wrong sub-strategy in consistent, fixable ways.
bullets: The obvious fixes — use a bigger model, or fine-tune the small one — cost money, data, or both
The paper asks: can a strong model fix a weak model's *process* instead of its *weights*?

slides.title: The Builder Writes Code, Routing Rules, and Format Contracts
slides.body: A strong 'builder' model is given the task family and a small validation slice, then iteratively authors a harness that wraps the weak 'target' model at inference time.
bullets: Harness = deterministic code + benchmark-specific routing + strict answer-format enforcement
Builder uses only 5% of the data as a validation set, refining the harness over multiple rounds
Once locked, the harness runs on the full test set — the target model's weights never change

slides.title: Example: A Weak Model Doing Theory-of-Mind Reasoning
slides.body: On a Theory-of-Mind benchmark (inferring what one character knows vs. another), the raw target model reasons inconsistently and sometimes answers in the wrong format entirely.
bullets: The harness intercepts the model's output, routes ambiguous cases to a deterministic sub-solver, and rejects/retries malformed answers
The target model still does the 'thinking' — the harness just stops its process errors from becoming task failures

slides.title: Nearly Double the Accuracy, Zero Parameter Updates
slides.body: Averaged across four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks:

slides.title: Where the Gains Actually Come From
slides.body: The paper is explicit about the mechanism — it isn't 'the model reasons more.'
bullets: Gains come from offloading unstable reasoning into deterministic code, not from longer chains of thought or more sampling
The weakest target models benefit the most — there's more process-error to remove
This makes it closer to a compiler pass over the model's behavior than a training technique

slides.title: When This Doesn't Help
slides.body: The setup has real constraints worth knowing before you reach for it.
bullets: You need a strong builder model available at authoring time — that's a real cost, even if it's paid once
Validated only on Theory-of-Mind benchmarks with clear, checkable structure; open-ended generation tasks may not have an equivalent 'deterministic harness' to write
A harness tuned tightly to a benchmark's format risks overfitting to that benchmark rather than the underlying skill

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Capability can transfer at test time through scaffolding, not just through weights
Deterministic code + routing + format enforcement fixed more errors than 'reason harder' would have
Cheap local models plus a well-built harness can close a surprising amount of the gap to bigger models

questions.prompt: In the paper's setup, what actually changes about the weak 'target' model?
options: Its weights are fine-tuned on the validation slice
Nothing — it's wrapped by an inference-time harness built by a stronger model
It's distilled into a smaller architecture
It's replaced by the builder model at test time
questions.explanation: The target model's parameters are never touched. All the gain comes from an external harness — code, routing, format rules — that the builder model authors around it.

questions.prompt: Where do most of the accuracy gains come from, according to the paper?
options: Encouraging the target model to sample more responses and vote
Giving the target model a longer chain-of-thought budget
Offloading unstable reasoning into deterministic code, routing, and format enforcement
Replacing the target model's tokenizer
questions.explanation: The authors are explicit that gains come from structural fixes — deterministic code and strict formatting — not from the target model reasoning more extensively or sampling more broadly.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of this approach highlighted by its setup?
options: It requires the target model's training data
It requires a strong builder model to author the harness, and was validated on structured Theory-of-Mind tasks specifically
It only works if both models have the same architecture
It cannot be evaluated on a held-out test set
questions.explanation: Authoring the harness needs a capable builder model, and the demonstrated results are on four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks with checkable structure — it's not yet shown to generalize to open-ended generation tasks.

posts.title: Qwen3.8-27B: A 27B Open Model That Runs on One GPU
posts.subtitle: Apache 2.0, 262K native context, native vision — and it beats Opus 4.6 Max on exactly one of five cited benchmarks.
posts.summary: Alibaba's Qwen team open-sourced Qwen3.8-27B on Aug 14, 2026: a dense 27B multimodal model under Apache 2.0 with 262K native context and a reasoning-effort dial, runnable on a single consumer GPU. It jumps sharply over its own predecessor and edges out Claude Opus 4.6 Max on one benchmark — but trails it clearly on most others.

slides.title: A Frontier-Adjacent Model You Can Run Locally
slides.body: Qwen3.8-27B — Alibaba Qwen, released Aug 14, 2026, Apache 2.0 license.
bullets: 27B dense parameters, native multimodal
#1 trending on Hugging Face within days, 3M+ downloads

slides.title: Open Models Usually Trade Capability for Size
slides.body: The most capable open-weight models have generally meant either mixture-of-experts giants or dense models too large for a single consumer GPU — pushing serious local use out of reach for most developers.
bullets: Running a frontier-adjacent open model at home usually meant multi-GPU setups or heavy quantization
Qwen3.8-27B targets that gap directly: strong benchmarks at a size that fits ~16-17GB of VRAM

slides.title: Dense 27B, 262K Context, a Reasoning Dial
slides.body: Rather than a mixture-of-experts design, Qwen3.8-27B is a dense multimodal model with a few notable specs.
bullets: 262,144-token native context, extendable to 1M tokens via YaRN
Native image and video understanding built in, not bolted on
A reasoning_effort parameter to trade latency/cost against answer quality per request
Weights released on Hugging Face and ModelScope under Apache 2.0

slides.title: A Large Jump Over Its Own Predecessor
slides.body: Alibaba's own benchmark comparisons show the biggest gains are relative to the prior Qwen generation, not necessarily against frontier proprietary models:

slides.title: Example: An Agentic Coding Task on a Single GPU
slides.body: A developer points Qwen3.8-27B at a repo through an agent harness for a multi-file coding task, running entirely on one consumer-grade GPU (~16-17GB).
bullets: The reasoning_effort dial lets them run cheap/fast for simple edits, then turn it up for a gnarly refactor
262K native context means most repos' relevant files fit without aggressive chunking

slides.title: The 'Beats Opus 4.6 Max' Headline Needs a Footnote
slides.body: Coverage highlighting Qwen3.8-27B beating Claude Opus 4.6 Max is accurate for exactly one benchmark, not a general claim.
bullets: On SWE-bench Pro, Qwen3.8-27B scores 61.7 vs. a cited 53.4 for Opus 4.6 Max — but that Opus figure is imported from Anthropic's own report, not rerun under Qwen's harness, so it isn't a fully controlled comparison
On HLE, Qwen3.8-27B trails clearly: 30.8 vs. 40.0 for Opus 4.6 Max
Some cited benchmarks (QwenSWEBench, CoWorkBench, RecreationBench) are Qwen's own, and don't yet have the external auditability of a mature public suite

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A genuinely strong open-weight jump for a size that fits one GPU — the predecessor-vs-new-version gains are the most solid numbers here
Treat 'beats a frontier proprietary model' claims benchmark-by-benchmark, not as a blanket statement
262K native context and a reasoning-effort dial make it a practical pick for local agentic workloads, not just a benchmark chart

questions.prompt: What architecture choice does Qwen3.8-27B make, compared to many other large open models?
options: It's a sparse mixture-of-experts model
It's a dense model, not mixture-of-experts
It's a retrieval-augmented model with no parameters of its own
It uses a diffusion-based text decoder
questions.explanation: Qwen3.8-27B is dense — all 27B parameters activate per token — which is part of why it fits on a single consumer GPU at this parameter count.

questions.prompt: On which cited benchmark does Qwen3.8-27B actually score above Claude Opus 4.6 Max?
options: HLE
SWE-bench Pro
All five cited benchmarks
None — it trails on every benchmark
questions.explanation: It scores 61.7 vs. a cited 53.4 on SWE-bench Pro — though that Opus figure is imported rather than rerun, so the comparison isn't fully controlled. It trails clearly on HLE (30.8 vs. 40.0).

options: Retrieval-augmented generation
A second, smaller summarizer model
YaRN-based context extension, up to 1M tokens
It cannot exceed its native context
questions.explanation: The model's native context is 262,144 tokens, extendable to 1M tokens via YaRN, a rotary-position-embedding scaling technique.

posts.title: MCP Resources: Context the App Attaches, Not the Model
posts.subtitle: The quiet MCP primitive: application-controlled data with URIs, push subscriptions, and — as of the 2026-07-28 spec — HTTP-style cache hints.
posts.summary: MCP splits context into three primitives by who decides: Tools are model-controlled, Prompts are user-controlled, and Resources are application-controlled. Resources give servers a way to expose addressable data — files, rows, active documents — that the host can attach, subscribe to, and now cache using spec-defined hints, without spending a model turn on a tool call.

slides.title: The MCP Primitive That Isn't a Tool Call
slides.body: Every MCP server can expose Tools, Prompts, and Resources. Resources are the one most tutorials skip — and the one that saves the most tokens.
bullets: Application-controlled, not model-controlled
Addressable by URI, readable on demand or by subscription

slides.title: Tools Are the Wrong Shape for 'Just Attach This File'
slides.body: If the host already knows the user has a file open, a database row selected, or a document active, routing that data through a tool call is wasteful.
bullets: A tool call spends a model turn deciding to call a tool, then another turn processing the result
The app already knows what context it wants attached — the model shouldn't have to ask for it

slides.title: Three Primitives, Three Different Controllers
slides.body: MCP's context surface splits cleanly by who decides it gets used:
bullets: Tools — model-controlled: the LLM decides when to call them, based on its own reasoning
Prompts — user-controlled: reusable templates the human explicitly selects (e.g. a slash command)
Resources — application-controlled: the host decides what to attach, list, or subscribe to

slides.title: resources/list and resources/read
slides.body: A server that supports resources responds to resources/list with the resources currently available, and to resources/read with their content.
bullets: Each resource has a URI (any scheme — file://, postgres://, custom), a name, a description, and a mimeType
Content comes back as text or a base64-encoded blob, matched to the mimeType
The host decides which listed resources to actually attach to the model's context — listing isn't attaching

slides.title: Subscriptions Turn Polling Into Push
slides.body: Servers declare a resources capability that can include listChanged and subscribe support.
bullets: resources/subscribe on a URI means the host gets notifications/resources/updated when that resource changes — no polling loop needed
notifications/resources/list_changed fires when the *set* of available resources changes (a file created, a table added)
This is what makes 'the model has live awareness of these three open files' cheap to implement

slides.title: Example: An IDE Exposing Open Tabs as Resources
slides.body: An IDE's MCP server exposes each open editor tab as a resource (file:///path/to/file.ts) rather than requiring the model to call a 'read_file' tool for each one.
bullets: The host subscribes to the active tab's URI
When the user edits and saves, the server pushes notifications/resources/updated — the host re-reads and refreshes the model's context automatically
No tool call, no extra model turn, no stale file content

slides.title: Tools vs. Resources vs. Prompts

rows: Take an action, fetch data on demand
Attach known context: files, rows, docs

slides.title: New in the 2026-07-28 Spec: Cache Hints
slides.body: resources/list and resources/read results can now carry ttlMs and cacheScope fields, modeled directly on HTTP Cache-Control.
bullets: A client can skip re-reading a resource it already has, until the ttlMs expires
cacheScope indicates whether that cached copy is safe to reuse across sessions or only within one
This matters for resources that rarely change (a schema) vs. ones that change constantly (an open file)

slides.title: When a Resource Is the Wrong Choice
slides.body: Resources aren't a universal replacement for tools.
bullets: If the model needs to decide *what* to fetch based on its own reasoning (search a query, pick a record), that's a Tool's job, not a Resource
The resources capability, including subscribe, is optional — plenty of clients don't support it yet, so don't design around push-only assumptions
Attaching a resource still consumes context window budget once it's in — a cache hint saves a re-fetch, not the tokens themselves

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Resources are for context the application already knows it wants attached — Tools are for context the model decides it needs
Subscriptions replace polling: subscribe once, get notified on change
The 2026-07-28 spec added HTTP-style cache hints (ttlMs, cacheScope) to cut redundant re-reads

questions.prompt: Who decides which Resources actually get attached to the model's context?
options: The model, via a tool call
The application/host
The end user, via a slash command
The MCP server, automatically, with no host involvement
questions.explanation: Resources are application-controlled: the host lists and reads them, then decides what to attach. This is the key distinction from Tools, which the model itself decides to invoke.

questions.prompt: How does an MCP client avoid polling a resource for changes?
options: It re-reads the resource on every model turn
It calls resources/subscribe on the URI and receives notifications/resources/updated when it changes
It's not possible — MCP has no notification mechanism
It relies on the model to ask periodically
questions.explanation: A server that declares subscribe support lets clients subscribe to a specific resource URI and get pushed notifications/resources/updated events instead of polling.

questions.prompt: What did the 2026-07-28 MCP spec add to resources/list and resources/read results?
options: A required binary format for all content
ttlMs and cacheScope fields modeled on HTTP Cache-Control
A mandatory authentication token per resource
Automatic translation between mimeTypes
questions.explanation: The 2026-07-28 spec added cache hints — ttlMs and cacheScope — so clients know how long a read stays valid and whether it's safe to reuse across sessions, cutting redundant re-fetches.
