posts.title: Mamba: Sequence Modeling Without Quadratic Attention
posts.subtitle: A selective state space that scans in linear time and still remembers what matters.
posts.summary: Mamba replaces self-attention's all-pairs comparison with a selective state space model: a recurrent state whose update rule is a function of the current token, giving linear-time compute and fixed-size memory — at the cost of exact long-range retrieval.

slides.title: Attention's O(n²) Problem, Solved Differently
bullets: Self-attention compares every token to every other token — cost grows quadratically with sequence length.
Mamba replaces that with a selective state space model (SSM): a recurrent state updated in linear time per token.

slides.title: Why Quadratic Attention Doesn't Scale
slides.body: Doubling context length quadruples attention's compute and memory. At very long contexts, the KV cache and attention matrix dominate cost long before parameter count does.
bullets: A 128K-token context needs roughly 16x the attention compute of an 8K context, for the same model.
Earlier linear-time alternatives (vanilla RNNs, linear attention) traded that cost away but lost selectivity — everything decays at the same fixed rate regardless of content.

slides.title: Selective State Spaces: Let the Input Choose the Decay
slides.body: Classic SSMs (S4) use fixed, input-independent transition matrices — efficient but unable to decide what to keep. Mamba makes the SSM's parameters (Δ, B, C) functions of the current input token.
bullets: Each token can write itself hard into the state, decay quickly, or pass through unchanged — recovering the content-based selectivity attention gets from softmax, without materializing an O(n²) matrix.
The recurrence is computed with a hardware-aware parallel scan, not step-by-step, so it still trains fast on GPUs despite being 'recurrent.'

slides.title: Attention vs. Selective State Space
slides.body: The headline win is inference: a fixed-size recurrent state means memory doesn't grow with context length the way a KV cache does.

slides.title: A Concrete Walkthrough
slides.body: Processing a 100K-token document: a Transformer keeps a KV cache entry for every one of those tokens, growing linearly and attended over quadratically each step.
bullets: Mamba keeps one fixed-size hidden state updated per token — the 100,001st token costs the same to process as the 2nd.
This is why Mamba-based and hybrid models get cited for cheap long-context inference rather than for raw benchmark accuracy alone.

slides.title: Where Mamba Falls Short
slides.body: Selectivity fixes the 'forget everything' problem, but a fixed-size state is still a bottleneck compared to attention's full lookback.
bullets: Tasks needing exact retrieval of one specific fact from far back in a long context (needle-in-a-haystack) tend to favor attention — Mamba must compress everything through its state.

Pure-SSM models have generally underperformed similarly-sized Transformers on some in-context-learning and copying benchmarks, which is why many production models hybridize Mamba layers with a few attention layers instead of going pure-SSM.
Don't reach for Mamba just for 'efficiency' on short, retrieval-heavy tasks — the win shows up at long sequence lengths.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Mamba trades attention's full pairwise comparison for a selective, input-dependent recurrent state — linear time, fixed memory.
The 'selective' part is the key idea: it recovers content-based reasoning that older RNNs and linear attention couldn't do.
Best used for long-context or streaming workloads, or hybridized with attention layers — not as a universal drop-in replacement.

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between Mamba's SSM and a classic (S4) state space model?
options: Mamba uses a much larger hidden state
Mamba's transition parameters (Δ, B, C) are functions of the input token, making the state update selective
Mamba removes the recurrent state entirely
Mamba only works on text, not other sequence types
questions.explanation: S4's transition matrices are fixed regardless of input; Mamba makes them input-dependent, so the model can choose what to remember or forget per token — that's the 'selective' in selective state space model.

questions.prompt: Why does Mamba's inference memory stay roughly constant as context length grows, unlike a Transformer's?
options: It uses quantization to compress the KV cache
It maintains one fixed-size recurrent state instead of a cache that grows with every token
It truncates old tokens after a fixed window
It runs on specialized hardware with more memory
questions.explanation: A Transformer's KV cache stores an entry per past token, growing linearly; Mamba compresses everything seen so far into one fixed-size state vector, so memory doesn't scale with sequence length.

questions.prompt: When should you be cautious about choosing a pure Mamba model over a Transformer?
options: When you need long-context efficiency
When the task requires exact retrieval of one specific fact from far back in a long context
When you want linear time complexity
When compute budget is limited
questions.explanation: Because Mamba compresses history into a fixed-size state, exact needle-in-haystack retrieval is harder than for attention, which can look back at every token directly — this is why many production systems hybridize Mamba with a few attention layers.

references.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces (arXiv:2312.00752)

posts.title: Prefill-Decode Disaggregation: Splitting Inference in Two
posts.subtitle: Why serving an LLM well means running two different machines, not one
posts.summary: Prefill (processing the prompt) is compute-bound; decode (generating tokens one at a time) is memory-bandwidth-bound. Running both on the same GPU pool means a burst of prompt processing stalls in-flight token generation. Prefill-decode disaggregation splits them into two independently-scheduled, independently-scaled GPU pools connected by a KV-cache handoff over a fast interconnect — trading a per-request network transfer for far more predictable latency and decoupled scaling knobs.

slides.title: Two Jobs Pretending to Be One
slides.body: Every LLM request actually runs two very different workloads back to back: reading the prompt (prefill) and generating tokens one at a time (decode). Serving them on the same GPU pool means picking one scheduling policy for two opposite bottlenecks.

slides.title: Prefill and Decode Fight Over the Same GPU
bullets: Prefill processes every prompt token in one batched forward pass — a large, dense matrix-multiply burst that's compute-bound and can saturate the GPU's FLOPs for the duration of that pass.
Decode generates a single new token per step, but each step still has to read the entire growing KV cache from GPU memory — it's memory-bandwidth-bound, with very little actual compute per step.
When both run on one shared pool (as in standard continuous batching), a new request's prefill burst competes for the same compute engines that in-flight decode steps need on every iteration.
The result is a stall: users mid-generation see their next token delayed because the GPU just got handed a large prompt to chew through — tail latency spikes exactly when the system looks busiest.

slides.title: Split Into Two Pools, Hand Off the KV Cache
bullets: Disaggregation runs prefill and decode as separately-scheduled worker pools instead of one shared pool — prefill workers only ever run the compute-heavy first pass over a prompt; decode workers only run the memory-bound, one-token-at-a-time loop.

Once a prefill worker finishes a prompt, it streams that request's freshly-computed KV cache to a decode worker over a fast interconnect (NVLink within a node, RDMA over InfiniBand across nodes) — the decode worker then owns the request for the rest of generation.

Each pool is provisioned for its own bottleneck: prefill favors raw FLOPs and can tolerate fewer, cheaper GPUs; decode favors HBM bandwidth and capacity to hold many concurrent requests' KV caches at once.
A router sits in front, assigning incoming requests to a prefill worker and then to whichever decode worker has spare capacity — replacing one monolithic batcher with two specialized ones.

slides.title: How One Request Actually Flows
bullets: 1. Router receives the request and assigns it to a prefill worker with available capacity.
2. The prefill worker runs a single forward pass over the whole prompt, producing the KV cache for every prompt token plus the first output token.
3. That KV cache is transferred to a decode worker over the interconnect — the prefill worker is now free to pick up the next request immediately.
4. The decode worker appends new KV entries and streams tokens back to the client one step at a time until it hits an end-of-sequence token or the length limit.

slides.title: Colocated vs. Disaggregated

rows: Compute-bound and bandwidth-bound work interleaved on the same hardware
Each pool tuned to a single, matching bottleneck
New prefill bursts can stall in-flight decode steps
Decode steps run undisturbed by incoming prompt traffic
KV cache must cross the network for every request
One batch size has to trade off both phases at once
Prefill and decode pools scale independently to match traffic mix

slides.title: Worked Example: A Mixed Traffic Batch
bullets: A service handles two traffic types at once: document summarization (a 6,000-token prompt, a short 100-token summary) and live chat (a 50-token prompt, a 500-token reply).

Colocated: the summarization request's 6,000-token prefill occupies the GPU's compute engines for one long burst — every chat request currently mid-decode has to wait out that burst before its next token lands, so chat users see a visible stutter.

Disaggregated: the summarization prompt's prefill runs entirely on a prefill-pool GPU while chat decode steps keep streaming smoothly on the decode pool; once prefill finishes, the summarization request's KV cache is handed off in one transfer and it starts decoding on its own worker.

Net effect: both request types get far more predictable latency, at the cost of one KV-cache transfer per request — including the short chat prompts, which now also pay that hop even though their own prefill was cheap.

slides.title: The Catch: Transfer Cost and Pool Sizing
bullets: The KV-cache handoff isn't free: for a large model, one request's KV cache can run to hundreds of megabytes, and every request pays this network hop — for very short prompts, the transfer overhead can exceed the compute the split saved.

Pool sizing depends on knowing the workload: if most traffic is short-prompt/long-output or the reverse, one pool ends up idle while the other is the actual bottleneck, so the split has to be re-tuned as traffic patterns shift.
Operational surface roughly doubles — two fleets to deploy, monitor, and autoscale, plus a KV-transfer path that has to stay fast and reliable or it becomes the new bottleneck itself.

When NOT to use it: small models or low-traffic services where a single GPU pool is rarely saturated by either phase — disaggregation adds cross-machine complexity and network cost without a real bottleneck to relieve; plain continuous batching on one pool stays simpler and cheaper.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Prefill (compute-bound, one burst per prompt) and decode (memory-bandwidth-bound, one token per step) are fundamentally different workloads that compete for the same GPU resources when colocated.
Disaggregation runs them as two independently-scheduled, independently-scaled pools, connected by a KV-cache handoff over a fast interconnect (NVLink or RDMA).
The payoff is more predictable tail latency and decoupled scaling knobs; the cost is a KV-cache transfer for every request and roughly double the operational surface to run.
It pays off at scale, with high traffic and heterogeneous prompt/output lengths — not for small deployments where a single GPU pool was never the bottleneck to begin with.

questions.prompt: Why do prefill and decode create opposite pressure on the same GPU?
options: Prefill is compute-bound processing the whole prompt in one burst; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, reading the KV cache once per generated token
Prefill uses more memory bandwidth than decode
They require completely different model weights
Decode performs more matrix multiplications than prefill
questions.explanation: Prefill runs one large batched forward pass over every prompt token, saturating compute. Decode does very little math per step but has to read the full, growing KV cache from memory on every single token — the two bottlenecks are opposite, and colocating them means one stalls the other.

questions.prompt: What has to be transferred from the prefill worker to the decode worker for each request?
options: The request's KV cache
The model's weights
The full training dataset
Nothing — they share GPU memory automatically
questions.explanation: Since a different physical worker now owns the rest of generation, the KV cache produced during prefill has to be streamed to a decode worker over a fast interconnect like NVLink or RDMA before decoding can continue.

questions.prompt: When is prefill-decode disaggregation a poor fit?
options: Low-traffic deployments where a single GPU pool is rarely saturated by either phase
High-traffic services with widely varying prompt and output lengths
Services that need predictable decode tail latency
Large-scale multi-tenant inference clusters
questions.explanation: At low traffic or with a small model, neither phase saturates the GPU on its own, so splitting adds cross-machine KV-transfer overhead and roughly doubles operational surface without relieving any real bottleneck.

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Buying Accuracy With Extra Tokens
posts.subtitle: Why reasoning models get smarter by thinking longer, not by growing bigger
posts.summary: Test-time compute scaling trades extra inference-time work for higher accuracy on an already-trained model: longer chains of thought (sequential scaling), more parallel samples combined by voting or a verifier (parallel scaling), or guided search over partial solutions. It doesn't change the model's weights or create new capability — it amplifies the odds of surfacing an answer the model could already produce, at a real and often multiplicative compute cost, and it pays off most on checkable, convergent tasks like math and code.

slides.title: More Thinking, Not More Parameters
slides.body: Test-time compute scaling trades inference-time compute for accuracy: instead of training a bigger model, you let an already-trained model spend more tokens — or more parallel attempts — before it commits to an answer.

slides.title: Pretraining Scaling Laws Hit a Wall
bullets: For years the dominant lever was pretraining scale — more parameters, more data, more compute, following predictable scaling-law curves — but each doubling gets more expensive and returns keep shrinking.
A standard transformer forward pass spends a fixed amount of compute per output token regardless of how hard the question is — a one-line arithmetic fact and a multi-step proof get the same budget.

That fixed budget caps how much genuine multi-step reasoning a single forward pass can do, no matter how large the model gets — there's no built-in mechanism to 'try again' or 'check the work' mid-pass.
Reasoning-heavy domains — competition math, multi-step code debugging, long-horizon planning — are exactly where this fixed-compute ceiling shows up as wrong answers, not just slow ones.

slides.title: Let the Model Spend a Variable Budget Per Answer
bullets: Sequential scaling: train the model (often via RL on outcome or process rewards) to emit a long chain-of-thought before its final answer — the model decides when to backtrack, double-check, or try a different approach.
Parallel scaling: sample the same prompt N times independently, then pick an answer via majority vote (self-consistency) or a learned verifier that scores each candidate.
Search: build a partial-solution tree and use a process reward model to guide which branches get expanded further, pruning weak paths instead of generating N full attempts blindly.
All three convert extra inference compute into higher accuracy on the same base model — the weights don't change, only how much work happens after the prompt is read.

slides.title: Sequential vs. Parallel: Different Costs, Different Failure Modes
bullets: Sequential (long CoT): one continuous stream of reasoning tokens — cost grows with output length, and so does wall-clock latency, since it's one autoregressive chain end to end.

Parallel (best-of-N / self-consistency): N independent samples that can run concurrently — latency can stay close to one generation given enough throughput, but cost scales roughly linearly with N, and you still need a way to pick the winner.

Picking the winner is the real bottleneck for parallel methods: majority vote only works when the correct answer is also the most common one, and a learned verifier is only as good as the process/outcome reward model that trained it.
Hybrid setups run several long-CoT samples in parallel and then vote or verify across them — combining both axes, at multiplied cost.

slides.title: Where Each Approach Pays Off

rows: N independent samples, no verifier needed
Short, checkable final answers (math, multiple choice)
N samples plus one scoring pass
Cases where the verifier is meaningfully cheaper or more reliable than generation
One long generation, cost scales with output length
Tasks needing genuine multi-step derivation, not just answer diversity
Large solution spaces where blind sampling wastes most attempts

slides.title: Worked Example: Self-Consistency on a Math Problem
bullets: Illustrative numbers, not a specific benchmark result: say a model gets a hard word problem right 35% of the time on a single greedy attempt.

Sample the same prompt 32 times at nonzero temperature and take the majority answer — accuracy on problems like this typically rises well above the single-sample rate, because independent wrong attempts tend to disagree with each other while correct attempts tend to converge on the same answer.

The gain isn't free or unlimited: it follows a curve of diminishing returns as N grows, and it assumes wrong answers are genuinely diverse — if the model has one confidently wrong reasoning path it repeats deterministically, more samples just repeat the same mistake.
This is why self-consistency works well for math and code (checkable, convergent answers) and works poorly for open-ended writing (no single 'correct' answer to converge on).

slides.title: The Catch: Compute Doesn't Buy Capability That Isn't There
bullets: Test-time compute amplifies a base model's existing ability to reach a correct answer sometimes — it can't manufacture a reasoning path the model never produces in any of its samples. If the correct chain of logic has near-zero probability under the model, more resampling won't reliably find it.
Cost is real and multiplicative: N samples means roughly N times the inference cost, which changes the economics of serving — a query that used to cost one forward pass can now cost dozens.

Latency and cost pull in different directions: parallel sampling can hide latency behind extra hardware, but sequential long-CoT can't — a longer chain is a longer wall-clock wait no matter how much hardware you throw at it.
Verifier quality caps the ceiling for best-of-N and search methods — a weak or biased reward model will confidently pick a wrong answer out of a candidate pool that contained the right one.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Test-time compute scaling trades extra inference-time work — longer reasoning chains, more parallel samples, or guided search — for higher accuracy, without retraining or growing the base model.
Sequential scaling (longer reasoning) and parallel scaling (more samples plus voting or verification) are the two main axes, and they compose.
It amplifies existing capability rather than creating new capability, and it multiplies inference cost — a deliberate accuracy-for-compute trade, not a free upgrade.
It pays off most on checkable, convergent tasks (math, code, structured reasoning) and least on open-ended tasks with no clear notion of a single correct answer.

questions.prompt: What is the core trade that test-time compute scaling makes?
options: Extra inference-time compute (longer reasoning, more samples) for higher accuracy, without changing model weights
Smaller model size for faster training
Lower precision weights for faster inference
More training data for better pretraining loss
questions.explanation: Test-time compute scaling leaves the trained weights untouched and instead spends more compute after the prompt is read — via longer reasoning chains, parallel samples, or search — to raise the odds of a correct answer.

questions.prompt: Why does self-consistency (majority vote over N samples) tend to work better on math problems than on open-ended creative writing?
options: Math problems have a single checkable correct answer that independent correct attempts converge on, while creative writing has no single 'correct' output to converge on
Math problems are always shorter, so sampling is cheaper
Creative writing models are never trained with reinforcement learning
Self-consistency only works with beam search, not sampling
questions.explanation: Majority voting relies on correct attempts converging on the same answer while wrong attempts disagree with each other — that assumption holds for checkable, convergent tasks like math and breaks down when there's no single ground-truth output.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of test-time compute scaling?
options: It cannot exceed the base model's existing ability to ever produce a correct reasoning path, and its gains come at a real, often multiplicative, inference cost
It requires retraining the model from scratch for every query
It only works on models under 1B parameters
It eliminates the need for any reward model or verifier
questions.explanation: More samples or a longer chain of thought can surface an answer the model was already capable of producing, but they can't manufacture a reasoning path with near-zero probability under the model, and the extra compute is a real cost multiplier on serving.

posts.title: Multi-Head Latent Attention: One Cache, Any Head
posts.subtitle: How DeepSeek shrinks the KV cache by caching one compressed vector instead of one per head
posts.summary: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2 and carried through DeepSeek's later models, caches a single low-rank latent vector per token instead of a separate key and value per attention head. A small decoupled slice still carries rotary position info at full size, and inference engines fold the reconstruction math into existing projections so decoding never materializes full per-head keys and values. The result is a KV cache close to a heavily-grouped GQA setup in size, without the quality hit GQA and MQA usually trade away.

slides.title: What If You Cached One Vector Instead of One Per Head?
slides.body: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses every token's key and value into a single small latent vector, then reconstructs per-head attention from it on the fly.

slides.title: GQA Shrinks the Cache — It Doesn't Change Its Shape
bullets: Standard multi-head attention (MHA) caches a distinct key and value vector per head, per token, per layer — cache size scales directly with head count.
Multi-Query Attention (MQA) shares one K/V pair across all heads, cutting the cache a lot but often costing model quality.
Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) groups heads into small clusters that share K/V — a tunable middle ground, and the default in models like Llama 3 and Mistral.
All three still cache full-width vectors per group. At long context lengths, reading that cache back from HBM — not the attention math itself — is what throttles decode speed.

slides.title: Compress the Content, Decouple the Position
bullets: MLA down-projects each token's hidden state into one small latent vector (c_KV) and caches only that — not separate per-head keys and values.
At attention time, learned up-projection matrices reconstruct per-head keys and values from the shared latent — one compressed vector expands back into every head's view.

Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) don't survive that compression cleanly: rotating a shared latent and then splitting it per head doesn't equal rotating each head's key first. MLA's fix is to decouple position from content — a small extra per-head slice is computed and cached at full size purely to carry RoPE's position signal, while the compressed latent carries content only.
So the cache holds two small pieces per token: the shared compressed latent, plus a tiny per-head positional slice — nowhere near the size of caching full keys and values per head.

slides.title: The Trick That Keeps Decoding Fast: Never Rebuild the Full Cache
bullets: Naively, you'd decompress the latent back into full per-head K/V at every decode step — expanding the compression you just did, and adding matrix multiplies to the critical path.

Inference engines instead absorb the up-projection matrices into the query and output projections algebraically, so attention scores are computed directly against the compressed latent — the full-size K/V is never materialized at all.
That absorption is why MLA's decode-time compute stays close to a low-rank operation instead of ballooning back to MHA-sized matrices — the compression is real, not just cosmetic in storage.
This is also why MLA isn't a drop-in kernel swap: serving it fast requires an inference engine (vLLM, SGLang, and similar) that implements this absorbed form, not just a generic attention kernel.

slides.title: Where MLA Sits Against MHA, MQA, and GQA

rows: Full K and V for every head
One shared K/V pair for all heads
Smallest cache, but often a real quality drop
K/V shared within small head groups
Tunable middle ground — group count trades cache size for quality
One shared low-rank latent + a small positional slice
DeepSeek-V2's reported design goal: cache footprint near a heavily-grouped GQA, quality at or above full MHA

slides.title: Worked Example: What Compression Actually Buys You
bullets: Illustrative numbers, not a specific model's real config: say a layer has 64 heads with head_dim 128. Full MHA caches 64 × 128 × 2 (K and V) = 16,384 values per token, per layer.
GQA with 8 groups cuts that 8x, to 2,048 values per token — still scales with group count.
MLA instead caches one shared latent of a few hundred values, plus a small fixed-size positional slice — independent of head count, because every head reconstructs from the same latent.

Multiply that per-token savings by every token in a long conversation or document, across every layer, and the difference decides how many concurrent long-context requests fit in a fixed amount of GPU memory.

slides.title: The Catch: This Isn't a Free Upgrade to an Existing Model
bullets: MLA changes the attention computation itself, not just how it's cached — you can't bolt it onto an already-trained MHA or GQA checkpoint the way you might swap a serving-side cache format.

A model has to be pretrained (or substantially adapted) with MLA's compress-then-reconstruct math from the start, which is a much bigger commitment than choosing a GQA group count at architecture-design time.
Fast serving depends on an inference engine that implements the weight-absorption trick — without it, naively decompressing the latent every step can erase the savings.
The decoupled positional slice means MLA doesn't shrink the cache as cleanly as the headline number suggests — there's a fixed per-head cost that doesn't go away.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: MLA caches one compressed latent vector per token instead of separate keys and values per head, reconstructing per-head attention from it at inference time.
A small decoupled slice carries rotary position info at full size because compression and RoPE don't commute — the rest of the savings come from the shared low-rank content.
Weight absorption is what makes it fast in practice: engines fold the reconstruction into existing projections so full-size keys and values are never rebuilt.
It's an architecture choice made at pretraining time, not a serving-side toggle — the payoff is a KV cache footprint closer to aggressive GQA, without GQA's usual quality tradeoff.

questions.prompt: What does Multi-Head Latent Attention cache per token, instead of a separate key and value per head?
options: Nothing — it recomputes attention from scratch every step
One shared low-rank latent vector, plus a small per-head positional slice
A quantized 4-bit version of the full multi-head cache
Only the value vectors, never the keys
questions.explanation: MLA down-projects each token into one compressed latent that all heads reconstruct from, plus a small decoupled slice that carries rotary position information at full size.

questions.prompt: Why does MLA need a separate 'decoupled' piece just for position information?
options: Because rotary position embeddings don't commute with reconstructing per-head keys from a shared compressed latent
Because position information is always cached uncompressed in every attention variant
Because MLA doesn't support long context windows
Because it's a leftover implementation detail with no technical reason
questions.explanation: Rotating a shared latent and then splitting it per head isn't equivalent to rotating each head's key individually, so MLA carries position via a small full-size per-head slice instead of through the compressed content.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of adopting MLA?
options: It only works on CPU inference
It requires pretraining (or substantial adaptation) with MLA's math from the start, and fast serving needs an engine that implements weight absorption
It increases the KV cache size compared to standard MHA
It eliminates the need for an attention mechanism entirely
questions.explanation: MLA is an architecture decision baked in at training time, not a serving-side cache format you can swap onto an existing checkpoint — and without an engine that absorbs the up-projection into existing weights, naive decompression can erase the cache savings.

posts.title: PagedAttention: Borrowing Virtual Memory to Fix KV Cache Waste
posts.subtitle: vLLM treats GPU memory like an OS treats RAM — pages, not one giant reserved slab
posts.summary: Naive LLM serving reserves one giant contiguous slab of GPU memory per request, sized for the worst case — and wastes most of it to fragmentation. PagedAttention borrows the operating system's virtual-memory trick: split the KV cache into fixed-size blocks, address them through a per-sequence block table, and let the attention kernel gather them on the fly. The payoff is memory waste that drops from the 60-80% typical of contiguous allocation to under 4%, plus the ability to share cache blocks across requests that partially overlap.

slides.title: The KV Cache Is the Real Memory Hog, Not the Weights
slides.body: Every token an LLM generates needs the key and value vectors of every prior token kept around for attention. For long sequences and large batches, this KV cache — not the model weights — is what actually runs a GPU out of memory. How you lay it out in memory decides how many requests you can serve at once.

slides.title: Contiguous Allocation Reserves for the Worst Case
bullets: Early LLM serving systems allocated each request's KV cache as one contiguous block of GPU memory, sized for the maximum sequence length the request could reach — even if the actual output ends up far shorter.

That over-reservation is internal fragmentation: memory sits allocated to a request but unused because the model stopped generating early. The vLLM paper measured 60-80% of allocated KV cache memory going to waste this way across real serving workloads.

Contiguous layout also blocks any sharing. If two requests share an identical prompt prefix (a system prompt, a few-shot example, parallel samples from one prompt), each still gets its own fully separate memory region — duplicating cache that is byte-for-byte identical.

The consequence compounds: memory waste caps how many sequences can be batched together at once, and batch size is the main lever for GPU throughput in LLM serving — so wasted memory directly costs served requests per second.

slides.title: Split the Cache Into Fixed-Size Blocks, Address Them Indirectly
bullets: PagedAttention (vLLM, Kwon et al.) divides each sequence's KV cache into fixed-size blocks — each holding the key/value vectors for a small, constant number of tokens — instead of one contiguous reservation.

A per-sequence block table maps logical block indices (block 0, 1, 2… of this sequence) to physical block locations anywhere in GPU memory, exactly like a page table maps virtual pages to physical frames in an OS.
Blocks are allocated on demand as generation produces new tokens, not upfront for a hypothetical maximum length — so a sequence that stops early never reserved memory it didn't use.
The attention kernel is rewritten to read key/value vectors through the block table's indirection, gathering scattered physical blocks at compute time instead of assuming one contiguous memory span.

slides.title: Indirection Also Buys Free Sharing
bullets: Because a logical block can point to any physical block, two sequences with an identical prefix can point their early logical blocks at the very same physical blocks — no copying, just two block-table entries referencing one region.
Parallel sampling (multiple completions from one prompt) and beam search are the direct beneficiaries: the shared prompt prefix's KV cache is written once and referenced by every branch.
When a shared block needs to diverge — one beam continues differently than another — vLLM uses copy-on-write: only that one block is duplicated at the moment of divergence, not the whole cache.

This mirrors exactly how an OS shares a read-only code segment across processes and copy-on-writes a page only when one process actually modifies it — PagedAttention imports the whole idea, not just the block-table part.

slides.title: Worked Example: Four Parallel Samples, One Shared Prefix
slides.body: A request asks for 4 sampled completions of the same 500-token prompt, each generating up to 200 more tokens.
bullets: Contiguous allocation: 4 independent reservations, each sized for 700 tokens worst case — the 500-token shared prompt gets stored 4 separate times, and any completion shorter than 200 tokens wastes the unused tail of its own slab.

PagedAttention: the ~500-token prompt occupies one set of physical blocks, referenced by all 4 block tables. Generation only allocates new blocks per branch as tokens are actually produced, and stops allocating the moment a branch finishes.

If the branches diverge after the first 50 generated tokens, only the blocks after that divergence point get copy-on-write duplicated — the prompt's blocks and the first 50 shared generated tokens stay shared across all 4.
Net effect on this single request: the prompt's memory footprint drops from 4x to 1x, and no branch ever reserves memory for tokens it never generates.

slides.title: Contiguous vs. Paged KV Cache

rows: Reserved upfront for max possible length
Not possible — each request fully separate
Gathers scattered physical blocks per lookup
Effective batch size at fixed memory
Higher — reclaimed memory serves more sequences

slides.title: What This Doesn't Fix, and What It Costs
bullets: PagedAttention addresses memory layout, not scheduling — it's complementary to, not a substitute for, continuous batching, which decides when requests enter and leave a running batch. vLLM uses both together.

Block-table indirection adds a real kernel cost: gathering scattered physical blocks is slower per memory access than reading one contiguous span, so the attention kernel itself has to be specifically written (and optimized) for gather-style reads.

Block size is a genuine tuning knob: small blocks maximize sharing granularity and minimize waste from partially-filled blocks, but increase block-table bookkeeping overhead; large blocks cut overhead but reintroduce some internal fragmentation in the last partially-used block per sequence.

When it matters less: for workloads dominated by a handful of very long, fully independent sequences with no shared prefixes and generous memory headroom, the fragmentation and sharing gains shrink — the win is largest precisely when batches are large and requests share structure.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: PagedAttention replaces one contiguous, worst-case-sized KV cache reservation per sequence with fixed-size blocks addressed through a per-sequence block table — the same virtual-memory idea an OS uses for RAM.

That indirection cuts typical memory waste from 60-80% down to under 4%, and as a side effect lets sequences with a shared prefix reference the same physical blocks, with copy-on-write only when they diverge.

It's a memory-layout fix, not a scheduling fix — it pairs with continuous batching rather than replacing it, and the gather-style attention kernel it requires is genuinely more complex than reading contiguous memory.

The gain scales with how much batches share structure and how tight memory headroom already is — it is the mechanism that made high-throughput, highly-batched LLM serving (vLLM) practical, not a universal speedup for every workload.

questions.prompt: What causes the 60-80% memory waste in contiguous KV cache allocation that PagedAttention targets?
options: The model weights are duplicated once per GPU
Each request reserves a contiguous block sized for the worst-case (maximum) sequence length, even if generation stops much earlier
The attention kernel recomputes keys and values for every new token
Every request must run on a separate GPU
questions.explanation: Contiguous allocation has to reserve for the worst case upfront because it can't grow a fixed memory span later — so memory sits allocated but unused whenever a sequence finishes shorter than its reserved maximum.

questions.prompt: How does PagedAttention let two sequences share an identical prompt prefix without duplicating memory?
options: It compresses the shared prefix using quantization
It reruns the forward pass once and broadcasts the result to both sequences
Each sequence's block table can point its logical blocks at the same physical blocks, with copy-on-write only when the sequences diverge
It merges the two requests into a single batch item until generation finishes
questions.explanation: Because blocks are addressed indirectly through a per-sequence block table, multiple sequences can reference the same physical block. Only the block where their outputs actually start to differ needs to be duplicated (copy-on-write).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what PagedAttention does NOT solve on its own?
options: It doesn't reduce KV cache memory waste from fragmentation
It doesn't decide which requests enter or leave the running batch — that's the job of continuous batching, which vLLM uses alongside it
It doesn't allow multiple sequences to share cache blocks
It doesn't work with beam search or parallel sampling
questions.explanation: PagedAttention is a memory-layout mechanism for the KV cache. Deciding when requests join or leave a batch is a separate scheduling concern, handled by continuous batching — vLLM runs both together.

posts.title: LLMRouter: One Framework to Stop Guessing Which Model to Call
posts.subtitle: 16+ routing strategies, one benchmark, a 14.6% jump over always calling your best model
posts.summary: LLMRouter, from UIUC's ULAB, is an open-source infrastructure library that unifies LLM routing — picking the right model per query instead of always calling the same one — as context encoders, model encoders, scoring functions, decision rules, and learning signals. Across its xRouteBench suite spanning QA, math, code, multimodal, and personalized tasks, learned routers beat the strongest single fixed-model baseline by 14.6% relative.

slides.title: Not Every Query Deserves Your Most Expensive Model
slides.body: LLMRouter (arXiv:2608.06867, UIUC's ULAB) is an open-source library that treats picking which LLM answers a query as its own trainable problem, not a hand-written if/else.

slides.title: No Single Model Is Optimal Across Every Query and Budget
bullets: Always calling the frontier model burns money on queries a small, cheap model would answer just as well.
Always calling a cheap model loses accuracy on the hard queries that actually need frontier reasoning.
Hand-tuned routing rules (regexes, keyword lists) don't generalize across task types, model updates, or cost budgets — they need constant manual retuning.
Most routing research reinvents its own benchmark and pipeline, so results across papers aren't comparable.

slides.title: Routing as a Sequential Decision, Not a Lookup Table
bullets: LLMRouter formalizes routing with five interchangeable pieces: a context encoder (represents the query), model encoders (represent each candidate LLM), a scoring function (predicts fit), a decision rule (turns scores into a pick), and a learning signal (what trains the whole thing).
That formulation covers single-turn routing, multi-turn conversations, and personalized routing under one interface instead of three separate systems.
Because the pieces are modular, a new routing idea only needs to swap one component — a new scoring function, say — rather than rebuild the whole pipeline.

slides.title: 16+ Routers, Five Categories, One Pipeline
bullets: Ships over 16 router implementations grouped into single-round (KNN, SVM, MLP, matrix factorization, Elo rating), multi-round, multimodal, agentic, and personalized routers.

A shared data pipeline extracts queries from benchmark datasets, builds embeddings for both queries and candidate models, then calls each candidate LLM to collect the performance data routers train on.
Ships with a CLI for training/inference, a Gradio chat UI, and an OpenAI-compatible API server — so a trained router can sit in front of real traffic, not just a notebook eval.

slides.title: Worked Example: A Mixed Batch of Queries
bullets: Feed the router a batch mixing easy arithmetic (GSM8K-style), a hard science question (GPQA-style), and a code-completion task (HumanEval-style).
A fixed-model baseline sends all three to the same model — overpaying on the arithmetic, or risking a wrong answer on the GPQA-style question if it picked cheap.

A trained router scores each query against its candidate pool and sends the arithmetic to a small fast model, the hard science question to a stronger one, and the code task to whichever candidate scored best on code — matching spend to difficulty per query instead of per deployment.

slides.title: Learned Routing vs. Always Calling One Model

rows: Every query goes to the same model
Strongest single model sets the floor
Per-query model selection, trained on performance data
Strongest gains under tight budgets or personalization needs

slides.title: A Router Is Only as Good as Its Candidate Pool and Its Training Data
bullets: Training a router requires actually calling every candidate model on labeled tasks first — building the training set costs real API spend before the router saves anything.
A router can't send traffic to a model that isn't in its candidate pool, and pools go stale as providers deprecate or reprice models — routers need periodic retraining, not one-time setup.
Multi-turn and personalized routing add real complexity: the router now has to track conversation state or per-user history, which is more that can drift or break silently.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: LLMRouter reframes 'which model should answer this' as a trainable, benchmarkable problem with a shared interface — not a bespoke script per team.
Learned routers beat the best single fixed model by 14.6% relative on xRouteBench, with lightweight and personalized variants doing best under tight cost budgets.
The real cost isn't running the router — it's building and maintaining the labeled data and candidate pool it depends on.
Open-sourcing the library (MIT license, 16+ routers, a shared benchmark) lowers the bar for teams to route by query instead of hardcoding one model for everything.

questions.prompt: What core idea does LLMRouter formalize?
options: A single best LLM that should handle every query
Routing as a modular pipeline of context encoders, model encoders, scoring functions, decision rules, and learning signals
A rule-based system of regex keyword matches
A method for compressing multiple LLMs into one smaller model
questions.explanation: LLMRouter unifies LLM routing into five interchangeable components, letting single-turn, multi-turn, and personalized routing share one framework instead of separate ad-hoc systems.

questions.prompt: On the xRouteBench evaluation, how did learned routers compare to the strongest fixed-model baseline?
options: They performed about the same
They underperformed by roughly 15%
They outperformed it by 14.6% relative
They were only tested on coding tasks

posts.title: KV Cache: Stop Recomputing Attention You Already Did
posts.subtitle: Every generated token reuses yesterday's Keys and Values instead of redoing them from scratch
posts.summary: Autoregressive decoding attends over every previous token to generate the next one. A naive implementation recomputes each past token's Key and Value projections at every single step, even though those vectors never change once computed. The KV cache stores them once per layer and per head, so each new step only computes Key/Value for the newest token — trading GPU memory that grows with context and batch size for compute that no longer grows quadratically.

slides.title: Generating Token 500 Shouldn't Redo Token 1's Work
slides.body: A transformer generates text one token at a time, and each new token attends over every token that came before it. Without a cache, that means recomputing the same Key and Value vectors over and over, once per remaining step.

slides.title: Naive Decoding Recomputes the Whole Prefix Every Step
bullets: At step t, generating the next token requires attention over all t previous tokens — which needs a Key and Value vector for each of them.
Once a token passes through a layer, its Key and Value vectors are fixed functions of that token — they never change on later steps.
A naive implementation ignores that and recomputes Key/Value projections for the entire prefix from scratch at every new step anyway.

Generating token 500 in a 500-token sequence redoes roughly 500× the projection work token 1 needed — total work across a full generation grows close to quadratically with sequence length from this alone.

slides.title: Cache Key and Value Once, Append the New Token Each Step
bullets: Each transformer layer keeps two growing tensors per sequence — a Key cache and a Value cache — filled in the first time each token passes through that layer.
On every new decoding step, the model computes Key and Value for only the newest token, appends them to the cache, and reuses everything already stored for every earlier position.
Attention now needs one new Query compared against a K/V cache that already holds every past position — no re-derivation required.

slides.title: One K/V Pair Per Layer, Per Attention Head
bullets: The cache is per-layer — a 32-layer model keeps 32 separate Key/Value caches — and per attention head within each layer.
Shape is roughly [batch, num_heads, sequence_length, head_dim] for both the Key cache and the Value cache.
Built during 'prefill' (the first pass over the whole prompt), then grows by exactly one position per token during 'decode.'
Reset when an unrelated new prompt starts, unless a separate technique like prompt/prefix caching reuses it across requests that share a prefix.

slides.title: Worked Example: A 7B Model at 4K Context
slides.body: Take a 32-layer, 32-head model with hidden size 4096 (head_dim 128), running in fp16.
bullets: K+V bytes per token = 2 (Key and Value) × 32 layers × 4096 hidden × 2 bytes ≈ 512 KiB per token.
At a 4,096-token context, that's roughly 512 KiB × 4096 ≈ 2 GiB per sequence — just for the cache, on top of the model weights themselves.
Serve 8 concurrent sequences at that context length and the KV cache alone costs on the order of 16 GiB — often more memory pressure than the weights.

slides.title: Per-Step Work, With and Without the Cache

rows: Every token in the prefix, again
Grows with context length × batch size

slides.title: The Cache Is Also the Memory Bottleneck
bullets: KV cache memory grows linearly with both context length and batch size — at long context or high concurrency it can exceed the model weights' own footprint.

That pressure is exactly what motivated techniques like Grouped-Query Attention (fewer shared K/V head groups) and paged memory management for the cache — cache size, not raw FLOPs, is often the real ceiling on how many requests a server can batch.
Quantizing the cache to int8 or fp8 trades a little accuracy for roughly half to a quarter the memory.
The cache is per-sequence — it can't be shared across unrelated requests unless they share an identical prompt prefix, which is a separate optimization on top of the cache itself.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: The KV cache trades memory for compute — turning per-step attention from redoing quadratic work into constant work per new token.
It stores Keys and Values (not Queries) for every past position, separately per layer and per attention head.
It's the single biggest reason autoregressive decoding is practical at production scale — and also the single biggest memory cost when serving long-context requests.
Techniques like Grouped-Query Attention, quantized caches, and paged memory management all exist to tame this cost, not to replace the cache itself.

questions.prompt: Why does naive autoregressive decoding redo work at every generation step?
options: Because the model's weights change after each token
Because it recomputes Key and Value projections for every previous token, even though those vectors never change once computed
Because tokenization happens fresh on every step
Because softmax must be recalculated over the entire vocabulary each step
questions.explanation: Once a token passes through a layer, its Key and Value vectors are fixed — a naive implementation ignores that and recomputes them for the whole prefix on every step instead of reusing what's already known.

questions.prompt: What exactly does the KV cache store?
options: The final output logits for each generated token
A copy of the model's weights per request
Each past token's Key and Value vectors, per layer and per attention head
The attention scores (softmax output) for every past step
questions.explanation: The cache holds Key and Value vectors — not Queries, weights, or attention scores — separately for each layer and head, so they can be reused instead of recomputed.

questions.prompt: What's the main tradeoff the KV cache introduces?
options: It makes generated text less accurate
It requires retraining the model from scratch
It trades GPU memory that grows with sequence length and batch size for less redundant compute
It only works for prompts under 512 tokens
questions.explanation: The cache eliminates redundant recomputation but must be stored in GPU memory, and that footprint grows with both context length and how many sequences are batched together — often the real ceiling on serving throughput.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Actually Sees
posts.subtitle: The context window is finite — what goes in it is now the job
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of deliberately curating everything an LLM sees on a given turn — system instructions, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and history — instead of treating the prompt as one fixed string. As agents run longer and accumulate more tool calls, what you keep, drop, summarize, or delegate away matters as much as what you ask.

slides.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Actually Sees
slides.body: Prompt engineering is one string. Context engineering is the whole information supply chain feeding a model on every turn — system instructions, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and conversation history.

slides.title: A Bigger Context Window Isn't a Free Lunch
slides.body: Every extra token in context costs latency and money to process, and it competes for the model's attention with everything else already there.
bullets: Models tend to weight information near the start and end of context more heavily than the middle — the well-documented 'lost in the middle' effect
An agent that keeps every past tool call verbatim can burn tens of thousands of tokens on stale file dumps and error logs before it reaches the actual question
Irrelevant or contradictory context doesn't just waste budget — it can actively pull the model toward a wrong answer

slides.title: Four Levers: Write, Select, Compress, Isolate
slides.body: Teams building long-running agents converge on the same four moves for managing context, regardless of which model or framework they use.
bullets: Write — save state outside the context window (a scratchpad file, a memory store) instead of re-deriving it every turn
Select — pull in only what's relevant right now, via retrieval or targeted tool calls, instead of dumping everything upfront
Compress — summarize or truncate what's no longer needed at full fidelity, keeping the gist and dropping the noise
Isolate — split work across sub-agents or sandboxes so one agent's noisy intermediate steps don't pollute another's context

slides.title: Compaction and Sub-Agent Isolation, in Practice
slides.body: Two concrete techniques for keeping context lean over a long agent run.
bullets: Compaction: once the context budget fills up, replace older turns with a structured summary — what was tried, what failed, what's still open — never dropping specific file paths or error messages the agent will need again
Sub-agent isolation: delegate noisy exploration to a separate agent and receive back a short digest, so one giant tool response never floods the parent conversation
Both trade overhead — compute to summarize, coordination to delegate — for a smaller, more focused context where the next decision actually gets made

slides.title: A Debugging Agent, Without and With Context Engineering
slides.body: Same task — fix a failing test — two very different context footprints.
bullets: Naive: read the whole repo into context, paste the full test output, paste every file the stack trace touches — tens of thousands of tokens before any reasoning starts
Engineered: grep for the failing assertion, open only the ~2 relevant files, keep a running 3-line log of what's been tried instead of full tool transcripts
The engineered version reaches the fix in far fewer tokens and is less likely to get distracted by code it never needed to see

slides.title: Prompt Engineering vs. Context Engineering

rows: Everything the model sees, turn over turn
An entire session or agent run
What to include, retrieve, summarize, or drop
Context rot: bloated, stale, or contradictory context

slides.title: Where Context Engineering Goes Wrong
bullets: Over-aggressive summarization can silently drop a detail the model needed three turns later — the failure shows up far from its actual cause, which makes it hard to debug
Retrieval-based selection can miss context that's clearly relevant to a person but doesn't match the query embedding closely
It adds real engineering surface area — memory stores, retrieval pipelines, sub-agent orchestration — that a short, one-shot task doesn't need
For small inputs and single-turn tasks, just putting everything in context is often simpler and cheaper than building a curation pipeline

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: The context window is a scarce, shared resource — treat what goes into it as a design decision, not an afterthought
Four levers cover most techniques: write state out, select only what's relevant, compress what's stale, isolate noisy work
Compaction must preserve specifics (paths, errors, decisions) — a lossy summary just moves the failure downstream
Match the effort to the task: long-running agents need real context engineering; short single-turn tasks usually don't

questions.prompt: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect?
options: A bug that crashes models on long inputs
The tendency for models to weight information near the start and end of context more than the middle
A technique for compressing context
A type of tokenizer error
questions.explanation: Models tend to attend most strongly to the beginning and end of their context, so relevant information buried in the middle of a long context is more likely to be underused — a key reason placement in context matters, not just presence.

questions.prompt: What does 'compaction' do in a long-running agent?
options: Deletes the system prompt
Compresses older turns into a structured summary while preserving key decisions and open threads
Reduces the model's parameter count
Increases the size of the context window
questions.explanation: Compaction replaces older conversation and tool history with a compressed summary once the context budget fills up, keeping the gist without carrying every raw token forward.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of over-aggressive summarization in context engineering?
options: It makes responses too verbose
It can silently drop a detail the model needs later, causing failures that are hard to trace back to their cause
It always increases API costs

questions.explanation: A dropped file path, variable name, or error detail doesn't fail loudly at the moment it's summarized away — it resurfaces later as a confused or wrong answer, far from where the information was actually lost.

posts.title: LoRA: Fine-Tuning Without Touching Most of the Weights
posts.subtitle: Freeze the model, learn a low-rank patch instead
posts.summary: LoRA freezes a pretrained model's weights entirely and learns a small low-rank update instead of retraining everything. It cuts trainable parameters by orders of magnitude, adds zero inference latency once merged, and is why serving many fine-tuned variants of one base model became cheap.

slides.title: LoRA: Fine-Tuning Without Touching Most of the Weights
slides.body: Full fine-tuning updates every weight in a model. LoRA freezes them all and learns a tiny low-rank patch instead — often under 1% of the parameters.

slides.title: Full Fine-Tuning Doesn't Scale Per Task
slides.body: Adam keeps two extra states per parameter (momentum and variance), so fine-tuning a 7B model in fp32 needs roughly 4x the parameter memory just for the optimizer — before activations.
bullets: A 7B-parameter model fully fine-tuned with Adam needs ~28GB just for optimizer states (fp32), on top of the weights and activations
Every downstream task needs its own full model copy to store and serve — expensive to keep and swap
Fine-tuning on a small dataset risks catastrophically overwriting general pretrained knowledge

slides.title: Freeze W, Learn a Low-Rank Delta Instead
slides.body: LoRA keeps the pretrained weight matrix W frozen and adds ΔW = BA, where B and A are much smaller matrices of rank r. Only B and A get trained.
bullets: For a weight matrix W of size d×d, B is d×r and A is r×d, with r commonly as small as 4-16
At inference, W' = W + BA is just a matrix add — no extra layers, no added latency
The original LoRA paper reports cutting trainable parameters by up to 10,000x and GPU memory by 3x versus full fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam

slides.title: Worked Example: Rank 8 on the Attention Projections
slides.body: Applying LoRA with rank r=8 only to the query and value projection matrices is the classic setup from the original paper — and it's enough to match full fine-tuning quality on many tasks.
bullets: For a 4096×4096 projection, full fine-tuning trains ~16.8M parameters; rank-8 LoRA trains 4096×8 + 8×4096 ≈ 65K — about 0.4% of that
Across an entire 7B model, LoRA adapters commonly total well under 1% of the base model's parameters
Only the tiny A/B matrices need checkpointing per task — swapping tasks means swapping megabytes, not gigabytes

slides.title: LoRA vs Full Fine-Tuning vs Adapter Layers
Where LoRA Struggles
bullets: Rank is a real tradeoff: too low underfits tasks needing substantial new knowledge; pushed too high, it approaches full fine-tuning's cost for little extra benefit
Training still runs a full forward and backward pass through the frozen base — LoRA saves memory and storage, not training-time compute
Works best when the target task is reasonably close to the pretraining distribution; large domain shifts often still need broader tuning
QLoRA extends the idea to a 4-bit quantized frozen base, trading a bit more compute for even lower memory

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Freeze the base model, train a low-rank delta — often under 1% of the parameters
Merged LoRA adds zero inference latency; adapter layers add a forward pass
Rank r is the main knob: small for cheap adaptation, larger when the task needs more capacity
One base model, many cheap LoRA adapters swapped in and out — that's the real unlock for serving many fine-tunes

questions.prompt: What does LoRA actually train?
options: The full weight matrix W
Two small low-rank matrices A and B, with W frozen
Only the model's biases
A separate full-size adapter model
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes the pretrained W entirely and learns ΔW = BA, where B and A are low-rank — that's the whole trainable set.

questions.prompt: Why does a merged LoRA adapter add no inference latency?
options: Because it only modifies the tokenizer
Because W' = W + BA is computed once and used like any other weight matrix
Because LoRA skips the attention layers entirely
Because it runs on a separate GPU in parallel
questions.explanation: Once training is done, B and A can be multiplied and added directly into W, producing a normal-sized weight matrix — no extra layers run at inference.

questions.prompt: What's the main tradeoff when picking the rank r?
options: Higher r always trains faster
Lower r always improves quality
Low r risks underfitting; high r approaches full fine-tuning's cost
Rank has no effect on results
questions.explanation: r controls how much capacity the low-rank update has — too small and it can't capture the task, too large and you lose most of LoRA's efficiency advantage.

posts.title: OpenART: Red-Teaming Agents With Environments That Evolve
posts.subtitle: 10,000+ stateful scenarios built to find the attacks static benchmarks miss
posts.summary: OpenART is a new open-ended arena for stress-testing AI agents across long, stateful tool-use sessions instead of short static prompts. Its evolutionary attack method hits an 85% pooled success rate across 75 agent-model configurations, with the widest gap over simpler baselines showing up on the hardest, longest-running tasks.

slides.title: OpenART: Red-Teaming Agents With Environments That Evolve
slides.body: Most AI safety benchmarks test one short exchange. Real agents run dozens of tool calls in a row, and risk can build up quietly across that whole session — OpenART is built to catch that.

slides.title: Static Benchmarks Miss Cumulative Risk
slides.body: Conventional red-teaming treats each prompt as independent. Agent behavior is mediated through shared state — files, memory, tool outputs — that gets modified and reused across a long-horizon workflow.
bullets: Short, static single-turn tests can't capture a risk that only emerges after many chained tool calls
OpenART's tasks require a median of 97 tool calls each — far beyond what one-shot prompt tests probe
The benchmark spans 10,000+ validated stateful scenarios across 50 domains, drawn from a pool of 500,000+ tools and skills

slides.title: EMHA: Let the Attack Evolve With the Environment
slides.body: Instead of a fixed jailbreak prompt, OpenART's Evolutionary Markov Hypergraph Attack (EMHA) evolves both the attack strategy and the environment together, searching for the sequences of tool calls that actually break an agent.
bullets: The environment itself is treated as evolvable, not fixed — new scenario variants get generated as weaknesses are found
Attacks are modeled over a hypergraph of possible agent-tool-state transitions rather than a single conversation thread
Evaluation spans 75 different agent-model configurations for a unified, comparable measure of robustness

slides.title: EMHA vs a Simpler Instruction-Only Baseline

rows: Pooled attack success rate (EMHA, all configs)
EMHA advantage over instruction-only evolution — simple environments
EMHA advantage over instruction-only evolution — complex environments

slides.title: The Kind of Scenario That Trips Agents Up
slides.body: Picture an agent given a long task in a simulated file-and-tool environment — nothing in any single step looks dangerous, but the state it accumulates over ~97 tool calls quietly narrows toward an unsafe action by the end.
bullets: No single tool call in the chain looks obviously adversarial in isolation
The risk is emergent from accumulated state, not from any one instruction — which is exactly what short static tests can't see
This is the gap EMHA is built to search for systematically instead of by hand

slides.title: Where This Kind of Benchmark Still Falls Short
bullets: It's a simulated arena — attack success in OpenART's environments doesn't automatically transfer 1:1 to production deployments
An 85% pooled ASR is an average across 75 configurations; individual agent-model pairs will vary a lot around that number
Benchmarks that measure attack success can themselves become optimization targets — a model tuned to score well on OpenART isn't guaranteed to be safer against attacks the benchmark doesn't cover
Generating 10,000+ validated scenarios is expensive; keeping the arena current as agents change requires ongoing investment

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Agent risk often builds up across a long tool-using session, not in any single step — that's what OpenART tests for
EMHA evolves the attack and the environment together instead of reusing a fixed jailbreak prompt
85% pooled attack success rate across 75 agent-model configurations, with the largest baseline gap on the hardest tasks
A high score here is a signal to investigate, not proof of real-world exploitability — sim-to-real gap still applies

They only work on text models, not agents
They require too much compute to run at all
questions.explanation: OpenART's tasks need a median of 97 tool calls — the kind of cumulative, stateful risk that a one-shot prompt test simply never triggers.

options: Only the attacker's prompt wording

Only the evaluation metric
questions.explanation: EMHA treats the environment as evolvable alongside the attack, generating new scenario variants as it searches for weaknesses — not just rewording a fixed jailbreak.

options: On the simplest environments

questions.explanation: The advantage grew from about 2 points on simple environments to over 17 points on the most complex ones — the harder the task, the more evolving the environment mattered.

posts.title: Tool Calling: How an LLM Actually Triggers a Function
posts.subtitle: The model never runs code — it emits structured JSON and a host process does the rest
posts.summary: Tool calling isn't the model reaching out and running code — it's the model emitting a structured JSON object that matches a schema you declared, which a host process intercepts, executes, and feeds back as a new message. The reliability comes from constrained decoding and a strict request/response loop, not from the model being smarter about APIs.

slides.title: The Model Never Touches a Single API
slides.body: Every 'agent calling a tool' is really the model predicting text that happens to look like a function call, and a separate program deciding to act on it.

slides.title: Free-Form Text Is a Terrible Interface for Actions
bullets: Early 'agents' asked the model to write prose like 'I should search for the weather in Austin' and then regex-parsed it — brittle, and one phrasing drift breaks the parser.
A model has no way to actually execute anything; it only predicts the next token. Without a strict contract, arguments come back malformed, quoted inconsistently, or with invented parameter names.
Hallucinated tools are the real risk: given no explicit list, a model will confidently invoke an API that doesn't exist, because 'a function that does X' is a plausible completion.

slides.title: You Declare a JSON Schema; the Model Fills It In
slides.body: Modern tool calling puts a machine-readable spec — name, description, and a JSON Schema for the arguments — into the request. The model is trained (and often decoding-constrained) to emit output matching that schema instead of prose whenever a tool fits.
bullets: The runtime, not the model, executes the call: it validates the JSON against the schema, runs the real function, and appends the result as a new 'tool' message in the conversation.
Constrained/grammar decoding masks out tokens that would produce invalid JSON at each step, so malformed output becomes a token-sampling impossibility rather than a hope.
The model only ever sees text: the tool definition going in, and the tool's result coming back as another message it reads like any other context.

slides.title: It's a Loop, Not a Single Call
bullets: 1) User message goes in with the list of available tools. 2) Model emits either a normal reply or a tool_call (name + JSON arguments). 3) Host executes it and appends a tool-result message. 4) Model resumes with that result in context — often producing another tool_call before ever answering.

Independent calls can run in parallel: if the model requests two tools with no data dependency between them, most runtimes fire both and merge the results back in before the next model turn — cutting round-trip latency roughly in half for that step.
Each round trip costs a full model inference pass, so a 4-tool-call chain isn't 'one request' — it's five: four tool turns plus the final synthesis.

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Independent Lookups
slides.body: Prompt: 'What's the weather in Austin, and what's 50 USD in EUR?' — two unrelated facts, so a well-built agent fires both tools in parallel rather than sequentially.
bullets: Turn 1 — model output: two tool_calls in the same message: get_weather({"city":"Austin"}) and convert_currency({"amount":50,"from":"USD","to":"EUR"}).
Host executes both concurrently, gets back {"tempF":91,"conditions":"sunny"} and {"result":46.10}, and appends both as tool-result messages tagged with matching call IDs.
Turn 2 — model reads both results in context and writes the final prose answer: 'It's 91°F and sunny in Austin; 50 USD is about €46.10.' No new tool calls needed.

slides.title: Prompted Parsing vs. Native Tool Calling

rows: Ad-hoc text pattern in the prompt
Structured field the API returns directly
Silently mis-parsed or crashes the parser
Rare — one action per text turn
Multiple tool_calls in a single turn
Standardized across most major model APIs

slides.title: Where It Still Breaks
bullets: Tool-selection accuracy degrades as the toolbox grows — past roughly a few dozen simultaneously offered tools, models start picking the wrong one or missing the right one, even with perfect schemas. Curate the set per-task instead of exposing everything at once.

A schema only constrains shape, not truth: the model can still fill valid JSON with a hallucinated argument value (a city that doesn't exist, an ID it invented), so the executing function still has to validate semantically.

Tool calling has no built-in permission model — anything declared as a tool is something the model will eventually try to call. Destructive tools (delete, send, pay) need an explicit confirmation step outside the loop, not just a well-worded description.

Don't reach for tool calling when the answer is already in the model's context or training knowledge — every call adds a full inference round trip's worth of latency and cost for something a direct answer would've solved instantly.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Tool calling = a JSON contract + constrained decoding + a host loop — the model still only predicts text, it never executes anything itself.
Independent tool calls can and should run in parallel; dependent ones force sequential round trips, each costing a full inference pass.
A valid schema guarantees well-formed arguments, not correct ones — always validate values, not just shape, before executing.
More tools isn't free: curate the offered set per task rather than exposing your entire API surface at once.

questions.prompt: What actually makes modern tool calling more reliable than the old 'parse the model's prose' approach?
options: The model has been given direct code-execution access
